docs.title: 前言
docs.text:
本书是一本开源免费的AI 时代计算机专业的学习体系指南，既是我献给学弟学妹的一份礼物，也是我为开源社区所做的一点绵薄之力。

如果这本指南能对大家哪怕一丝一毫的帮助，都是对我极大的鼓励和慰藉。

本书目前包含了以下部分（如果你有更好的建议，或者想加入贡献者行列，欢迎通过邮箱 zhangchaowen@stu.scu.edu.cn联系我，或者在 Issue 中提出）：

  • 本书使用指南：由于书内涵盖资源众多，我根据不同人群的空闲时间和学习目标制定了对应的使用指南。
  • AICS学习规划：一份仅供参考的AICS学习规划

docs.title: 星光启程的地方
docs.text:
入学时我是一个对计算机一窍不通的小白，除了玩过电脑游戏，我甚至不会下载正规的软件。但我还是怀着新奇和热情开始了我的计算机科学之路。每天我都会按时去教室，认真听取老师的讲课，做好笔记，然后完成任务。然而，我逐渐发现，每个老师的教学方式不同，速度不同，侧重点不同，热情不同。有的仅仅是照着陈旧的ppt复述，有的仅仅是增加了抽人回答ppt上的问题，真正热情投入教育让学生批判性思考的非常少，就这样日复一日的枯燥学习中，我的热情逐渐被消磨.....因为这样，我曾陷入迷茫，我一度怀疑我是不是不适合学计算机，因为童年对于极客的所有想象，已经被我第一个学年的体验彻底粉碎了。我时常问自己，AI既然能做这么多，我究竟应该掌握什么知识？我还需要学习Java、Python吗？我还需要去学习数据结构、计算机网络吗？我本以为我的大学会这样平淡度过，上课、学习、娱乐。没两个月，DeepSeek-V3横空出世了。身边所有的人都在吹嘘这个出生不久的AI模型。

作为小白的我认为这没什么，只是多了一个能帮助我编写代码的工具。我仍然想往常一样，按照计算机四大件的顺序啃教材。直到快进入大二，一次偶然的机会，我的数据结构老师在群里发了一篇帖子，那是Andrew Ng在Buildathon上的演讲稿。看到帖子的第一眼我便被深深吸住了，我一口气看完了全部内容，仍不满足的我又去Youtube观看了演讲原视频。

演讲围绕AI辅助编程、快速开发产品原型，以及AI工程师技能需求，这让我真正看到了这个行业乃至所有行业未来的趋势--理解AI并掌握AI。

在吴恩达的演讲里，我整理了几个重要思想：

  • “快速行动，承担责任”。AI辅助编程让独立原型开发实现10倍加速。原型成本大幅降低使快速多次试错成为可行策略，真正价值在于在试错中发现值得深度开发的项目。

  • 代码正在贬值，开发者需要转型为系统设计者和AI指挥者。编程工具已经历多代进化：从GitHub Copilot到IDE，再到高度代理化的程助手。工具迭代速度创造实质性效率差距，落后半代即可能显著影响产出能力。代码价值本身正在降低。AI可自动生成代码、迁移数据库架构，使架构决策变得更可逆。开发者需要从代码编写者转型为系统设计者和AI指挥者，重点把控核心架构与复合型系统构建。

  • “AI时代无需学编程”是史上最糟的职业建议。吴恩达强烈反对“AI时代无需学编程”的观点，指出历史上每次编程工具进步都让更多人群具备编程能力。他团队中的CFO、法律顾问、前台人员均通过学习编程提升工作效率。未来核心技能是“精准告诉计算机该做什么”，这需要理解计算机语言与编程逻辑。非技术人员可通过AI辅助快速掌握基础编程能力，实现跨领域效率提升。

  • AI工程师奇缺，大学课程却已严重脱节。计算机专业毕业生失业率升至7%，可企业却仍面临AI工程师严重短缺。核心矛盾在于大学课程未能及时覆盖关键技能：AI辅助编程、大语言模型调用、RAG/Agentic工作流构建、规范错误分析流程等。新兴AI工程师需掌握三大技能：使用最新AI编程工具、熟悉AI构建模块（提示工程/评估技术/MCP）、具备快速原型能力与基础产品直觉。

后来，我按照Andrew Ng教授的建议，在这些方向上开始自学。我逐渐放弃了大学的课堂，并在此期间找到了很多优质的课程资源。在这样的课程中，你完全不需要任何顾虑，只需要努力、认真、花时间就够了。此前在课堂上那种有劲没处使的感觉，那种付出再多时间却得不到回报的感觉，从此烟消云散。这太适合我了，我从此爱上了自学。

如果你也在苦恼地学习计算机知识，和我有着同样的困惑，不妨去看看吴恩达教授在 Buildathon 上的演讲，因为那是我最初心动的地方。

docs.title: 为什么写这本书
docs.text:
大二秋季学期学习操作系统时，我发现老师讲得极其枯燥，很多例子是十年前的，实验课指南更是 13 年前的。后来和身边朋友交谈，我也能感受到大家对 AI 快速发展的担忧和对未来就业的焦虑。那时候我已经自学一年多了，整理了很多资源，便分享给了朋友们——毕竟，谁不希望快乐地度过大学时光，还能找到好工作或考上研究生呢？

随着又一年的积累，资源内容已经相当丰富，基本覆盖了计科、智能系、软工系的绝大多数课程。我也为每个课程建了各自的 GitHub 仓库，汇总自学资料及作业实现。直到后来计算学分时，我打开自己的培养方案，发现它已经是我这个自学仓库的子集了——而这距离我开始自学也才两年而已。于是，一个大胆的想法在我脑海中浮现：也许我可以打造一个自学式的培养方案，把这三年自学中遇到的坑、走过的路记录下来，同时结合对 AI 时代的思考，为后来的 CSers 贡献一份微薄之力。

docs.title: 自学还是？
docs.text:
自学最大的好处在于可以完全根据自己的进度来调整学习速度。你可以随时改变学习计划，按照自己的节奏来，而不是局限在培养方案和课堂里。

自学的另一个好处是博采众长。我第一次在笔记本装双系统时就犯了错，把 Windows 给抹掉了。唯一庆幸的是当时没有什么贵重资料。后来又了解到现代固态硬盘不会彻底消除数据，只要新系统没有占用原有磁盘的那部分空间，就有可能恢复数据。正是这些试错，让我不断学到各种平时接触不到的知识。

自学的第三个好处是时间自由。大学本就相对自由，自学更是可以安排自己的学习时间和计划。只要时间安排得当，你仍然能一边自学，一边取得好成绩。

自学有什么坏处吗？当然，凡事有利有弊。

第一个坏处是不便沟通。你遇到的问题，未必有人遇到，也未必有人感兴趣。不过，善于借助 Google、StackOverflow 和 AI 等平台提问，可以解决 90% 的问题。第二个坏处是很多优质课程和资源是英文的，但这已经不是什么大问题了，如今翻译软件和插件几乎完美解决了这个问题。第三个，也是最难的——自律。没有 DDL 真是一件可怕的事，随着学习内容深入，难度也会上升，坚持学完整个课程是相当虐的。你得有足够的驱动力强迫自己静下心来，理解上千行的代码框架，忍受数个小时的 debug 时光。而这一切，没有学分，没有绩点，没有老师，没有同学，只有一个信念——你在变强。

docs.title: 这本书为谁而写
docs.text: 任何有志于学好用好计算机知识的朋友都可以参考这本书。如果你已经有了一定的计算机基础，只是对某个特定领域感兴趣，可以挑选感兴趣的内容进行学习。当然，如果你像我当年一样对计算机一无所知，初入大学校门，我希望这本书能成为你的攻略，让你花最少的时间掌握所需的知识和能力。某种程度上，这本书更像是一个根据我的体验来排序的课程搜索引擎，帮助大家足不出户体验优质计算机课程。

docs.title: 特别鸣谢
docs.text: 在这里，我怀着崇敬之心真诚地感谢所有将课程资源无偿开源的教授和开发者们。这些课程和资源倾注了他们数十年教学的积淀和心血，他们却选择无私地让所有人享受到如此高质量的 CS 教育。没有他们，我的大学生活不会这样充实而快乐。很多教授在收到我的感谢邮件后，甚至会回复上百字的长文，真的让我无比感动。他们时刻激励着我：做一件事，就得用心做好，无论是学习、科研，还是为人。

docs.title: 加入贡献者行列
docs.text: 一个人的力量终究是有限的。这本书是我在繁重的科研之余熬夜抽空写出来的，难免有不够完善之处。另外，由于我个人做的是计算机应用方向，很多课程侧重应用实践，对数学、理论计算机、高级算法相关的内容则相对少些。如果你在其他领域有丰富的自学经历与资源，欢迎直接在项目中发起 Pull Request，也可以通过邮件联系我（zhangchaowen@stu.scu.edu.cn）。

docs.title: 关于交流群
docs.text: 本书支持页面评论功能。如果你想自学某门课程，可以建立群聊（QQ 或微信皆可），然后在对应课程页面下方发表评论，注明学习目标和加入方式。此外，过去已有不少朋友在 Issue 中建立了交流群，可以直接加入。

docs.title: 请作者喝杯下午茶
docs.text: 本书内容完全开源免费。如果你觉得这个项目对你有帮助，可以给仓库点个 star，或者请作者喝一杯下午茶。

docs.title: 一份仅供参考的学习规划
docs.text:
本指南旨在构建一套面向 AI 时代的计算机科学学习体系，帮助计算机专业初学者建立系统的知识结构，掌握现代软件工程与 AI 应用开发能力，并找到适合自己的专业发展方向。

这份指南并非要求所有学习者按照固定顺序完成全部课程。你可以根据自己的知识基础、学习阶段和发展目标，选择适合自己的学习路径。

docs.title: 工具和技能
docs.text:
工欲善其事，必先利其器。

工具和技能是学校很少教授的东西，但却是提升工作学习效率的必备。

工具或技能 说明 学会提问 学会提问，如果你刚接触到这个专业，你可能根本不会正确提问，遇到问题先问AI，使用搜索引擎，直到最后再去麻烦别人，这里推荐阅读提问的智慧这篇文章，学会真正的提问方式。 魔法（科学上网） 由于一些众所周知的原因，谷歌、GitHub 等网站在大陆无法访问，这也导致我们无法获得一些需要的资源，这时候就需要使用一点点魔法（科学上网）。 shell 命令行（shell）是一门被忽略的技能，但实际上，它会极大地提高你作为工程师的灵活性以及生产力，命令行的艺术是一份非常经典的教程，强烈推荐大家掌握一些基本的shell命令。 开发环境和编辑器 开发环境是程序员工作的必备环境，如果你是 Mac 用户，那么你很幸运，这份指南 将会手把手地带你搭建起整套开发环境。如果你是 Windows 用户，在开源社区的努力下，你同样可以获得与其他平台类似的体验：Scoop。现如今我们更多的是使用Visual Studio这样的集成开发环境，其中最著名的是VS Code，在VS Code中，我们可以使用各种插件配置一个好的开发环境提升我们的开发效率。 编程语言的开发工具链 编译器、包管理、依赖与构建工具。尽管如今的IDE已经有很强大的功能，能够一键打包运行代码，但是某些情况下（例如了解代码构建原理，或是追求极致的构建效率）我们仍然需要使用编程语言的开发工具链，例如GNU Make是一款工程构建工具，善用 GNU Make 会让你养成代码模块化的习惯，同时也能让你熟悉一些大型工程的编译链接流程。 Git 版本控制、分支合并、PR 与协作流程。一款代码版本控制工具。Git一定是每个学 CS 的童鞋必须掌握的神器之一。 Markdown 编写 README、笔记与技术文档。计算机行业最常用的文档格式，学会后你便拥有极致的编排文档的能力。 Docker 容器化开发环境与镜像部署。一款相较于虚拟机更轻量级的软件打包与环境部署工具。 Vim/Emacs 高效终端编辑器与远程开发。Vim是一款命令行编辑工具，它能够极大地提高你的开发效率；Emacs是与 Vim 齐名的经典编辑器，同样具有极高的开发效率，同时具有更为强大的扩展性。 Latex 学术论文与规范化文档排版。逼格提升 论文排版工具。

docs.title: 计算机科学基础
docs.text:
九层之台，起于累土。

计算机科学基础是所有上层能力的共同地基，也是 AI 最难替你补上的部分。代码可以生成，但对原理的理解不能外包：遇到性能瓶颈、诡异的并发问题或者线上故障时，能救你的恰恰是操作系统、网络、数据结构这些“老知识”。建议先广后深，下面每门课都附了该领域的经典课程与教材，不必全部学完，选一条适合自己的线路走通即可。

课程 说明 数学基础 微积分、线性代数、离散数学。数学决定了你在这一行能走多远：微积分是理解梯度与优化的入口，线代是所有机器学习和图形学的语言，离散数学则是算法、密码学与编译理论的共同底座。建议在大一就把微积分和线代学到“刻骨铭心”的程度，而不是考完就忘，如果课上讲得晦涩，可以参考 MIT 18.06 的公开课程，以及 3Blue1Brown 那些把数学本质讲得极具美感的动画视频。 程序设计基础 C/C++、Java、Python。编程语言是工具，重要的是理解语言背后的设计思想：数组、字符串、指针、面向对象。初学者不要同时学好几门语言，先深入一门，再通过第二门理解不同的编程范式与生态，会比“每门都学过一点”走得更远。 数据结构和算法 算法是计算机科学的核心，是面试和刷题绕不开的内容，也是几乎一切专业课程的基础。如何将实际问题通过数学抽象转化为算法问题，并选用合适的数据结构在时间和内存大小的限制下将其解决是算法课的永恒主题。零基础入门可先用《Hello 算法》建立直观理解，详见 ALGO-101：Hello 算法。 数字逻辑与计算机组成 逻辑电路、CPU、指令与存储层次。这一块回答一个朴素的问题：程序到底是怎么跑起来的。想要既有趣又完整地建立这套认知，很推荐从零开始造一台计算机的 Nand2Tetris 入门，再深入 UCB CS61C 这类体系结构课程。 操作系统 操作系统把复杂而混乱的硬件虚拟成一套优雅的抽象，是所有应用的共同底座。这门课真正的收获往往来自动手，没有什么比亲手写一个内核更能加深理解，这里推荐MIT 6.S081 (基于 xv6)以及仓库来学习。 计算机网络 大名鼎鼎的 Stanford CS144: Computer Network，8 个 Project 带你实现整个 TCP/IP 协议栈。如果你只是想在理论上对计算机网络有所了解，那么推荐阅读 UCB CS168 这门课程配套的教材。 数据库系统 CMU 的著名数据库神课 CMU 15-445: Introduction to Database System 会通过 4 个 Project 带你为一个用于教学的关系型数据库 bustub 添加各种功能。实验的评测框架也免费开源了，非常适合大家自学。此外课程实验会用到 C++11 的众多新特性，也是一个锻炼 C++ 代码能力的好机会。 编译原理与程序语言 理论学习推荐阅读大名鼎鼎的《龙书》。当然动手实践才是掌握编译原理最好的方式，推荐北京大学编译原理实践课程，丰富的实验配套和循序渐进的文档带你实现一个类C语言到 RISC-V 汇编的编译器。当然编译原理课程目录下也有众多其他优质实验供你选择。 软件工程 一份“能跑”的代码，和一份高质量的工业级代码是有本质区别的。我推荐的是伯克利的 UCB CS169: software engineering。但需要提醒的是，和大多学校（包括贵校）的软件工程课程不同，这门课不会涉及传统的 design and document 模式，即强调各种类图、流程图及文档设计，而是采用近些年流行起来的小团队快速迭代 Agile Development 开发模式以及利用云平台的 Software as a service 服务模式。 计算理论与人工智能基础 可计算性、复杂度、AI 与机器学习基础。这一部分偏理论，但它给你的是边界感：哪些问题根本上算不出来，哪些问题算得出来但代价高到不可接受，为什么有些优化注定徒劳。同时它也是理解现代 AI 的起点，帮助你看清传统人工智能、机器学习与深度学习之间的关系与差异，避免在技术热潮里只记得工具名字，却说不清它们解决了什么。

docs.title: AI 时代工程能力
docs.text:
君子生非异也，善假于物也。

这一节与传统培养方案差别最大，但不意味着可以跳过基础。课程分两条线：一条用 AI 提效，写代码、查 bug、读源码都更快；另一条用 AI 造东西，把模型、检索与工具调用组合成可用的应用。Prompt 谁都能写，难的是让系统稳定、可评估、可监控、成本可控。

课程 说明 AI 与 LLM 基础 模型原理、Token、Embedding、能力边界。推荐卡帕西（Karpathy）的 Neural Networks: Zero to Hero 从零手写 GPT，以及 《动手学深度学习》。 提示工程 指令设计、结构化输出、工具调用与提示评估。推荐读读 《提示工程指南》，再用一批测试样本对比效果。 AI 辅助学习 用 AI 阅读教材、源码与论文，并独立核验与验证。让 AI 解释、追问反例、自己动手验证，避免“好像懂了”的错觉。 AI 辅助软件开发 AI 编程工具、Agent 驱动的软件开发、工程化方法。可从 Claude Code、Codex、DeepSeek Harness入手。 AI 辅助软件工程 需求、设计、测试、审查、迁移与 CI/CD。把 AI 放进整个软件生命周期，而不只是敲代码那一步。 大模型应用开发 LLM API、流式输出、结构化响应、RAG 与 Agent 应用。入门推荐跟着 Anthropic 的课程 逐行跑一遍示例。 检索增强生成与知识工程 文档切分、检索、重排、RAG 评估与 GraphRAG。动手搭一套文档问答，并用评估数据集验证检索效果，可参考 LlamaIndex。 智能体工程 规划、工具调用、记忆、多 Agent 与安全部署。推荐阅读 Building Effective Agents。 AI 评估与可观测性 评估数据集、LLM 评审、Tracing 与错误分析。没有评估就无法判断改动好坏，工具可看 Ragas 与 Langfuse。 AI 应用部署工程 服务部署、并发流式、监控、成本与模型回滚。最快的成长方式是把小项目真正部署上线并交给别人使用。

docs.title: 专业方向
docs.text:
闻道有先后，术业有专攻。

没有人在本科阶段能把所有方向学一遍，也不必如此。建议以兴趣、科研目标和就业规划的交集为准，选定一到两个方向持续深入。入门标准很朴素：能读懂经典论文、能复现一个小实验、能说清该方向的核心问题与权衡。暂时没想清楚也不要焦虑，把基础打扎实，大多数方向的大门都会为你打开。

课程 说明 人工智能与机器学习 深度学习、强化学习、LLM 与多模态。入门推荐 吴恩达的 Machine Learning Specialization，再深入 CS231n 与 CS224n。 软件工程与应用开发 前后端、全栈、架构与云原生开发。入门可从 The Odin Project 或 Full Stack Open 开始，边写边部署。 计算机系统 体系结构、编译、并行与内核开发。推荐 UCB CS61C 与被誉为神书的 CSAPP，并行方向看 CMU 15-418。 分布式系统与云计算 一致性、共识、算法与大规模系统设计。首选 MIT 6.5840，5 个 Lab 带你实现基于 Raft 的 KV 存储。 计算机网络与信息安全 网络协议、密码学、Web 与系统安全。理论基础看 UCB CS161，动手实验跟 SEED Labs。 计算机视觉 图像处理、检测分割、3D 视觉与视频。入门神课 Stanford CS231n，作业从零实现反向传播与卷积。 自然语言处理 语言模型、序列建模、信息抽取与检索。推荐 Stanford CS224n，进阶读 Hugging Face 的 NLP Course。 机器人与自主系统 运动规划、控制、SLAM 与自动驾驶。入门看宾大的 Robotics Specialization，SLAM 读高翔的《视觉 SLAM 十四讲》。 计算机图形学与游戏开发 渲染、光线追踪、着色器与游戏引擎。入门首选 UCB CS184，进阶做一遍 《Ray Tracing in One Weekend》。 数据科学与大数据 数据分析、挖掘、数据工程与流处理。从 Kaggle Learn 快速上手并打一场比赛，数据工程看 data-engineering-zoomcamp。

docs.title: 职业发展与就业
docs.text:
不患无位，患所以立。

技术和岗位不是一回事：会写代码的人多，能讲清自己做过什么、为什么这么做的人少。这一节的核心是把学习成果转化为证据，包括能跑的项目、可读的仓库、清楚的文档，以及面试中讲明技术选择的能力。尽早开始积累，实习和求职的准备往往需要几个学期，而不是临时抱佛脚。

课程 说明 职业方向认知 了解各类岗位职责与能力要求。多读招聘网站的 JD，参考 levels.fyi 看清各岗位的职级要求。 项目经验与作品集 项目选题、部署演示、GitHub 与技术博客。一个能点开、能运行、讲得清楚的项目，比“熟悉 XX 技术”更有说服力。 实习与求职准备 简历、算法与工程面试、系统设计面试。算法刷 LeetCode，系统设计必读 System Design Primer。 科研与学术发展 文献阅读、实验复现、论文写作与申请。入门读 《How to Read a Paper》，文献管理用 Zotero，排版用 LaTeX。 技术沟通与团队协作 文档编写、代码审查、项目管理与表达。推荐 Google 的 Technical Writing Courses 与 工程实践文档。 持续学习与职业成长 跟踪技术趋势、评估新技术、长期规划。读官方文档而非二手教程，关注 Hacker News 保持输入。

docs.title: 定制路线
docs.text:
授人以鱼不如授人以渔

以上的课程规划难免带有强烈的个人偏好，不一定适合所有人，更多是起到抛砖引玉的作用。如果你想挑选自己感兴趣的方向和内容加以学习，可以参考我在下面列出来的资源。

  • MIT OpenCourseWare: 麻省理工学院的课程资源开放共享项目，收录了数以千计的各科课程资源，其中计算机类的课号是 6.xxx。

  • UC Berkeley EECS Course Map: UC Berkeley 的 EECS 培养方案，以课程地图的方式将各门课程的类别和先修关系一目了然地呈现，其中绝大多数课程本书中均有收录。
  • UC Berkeley CS Course List: UC Berkeley 的 CS 课程列表。
  • Stanford CS Course List: 斯坦福的 CS 课程列表。

docs.title: 如何使用这本书
docs.text: 随着贡献者的不断增多，本书的内容也不断扩展，想把书中所有的课程全部学完是不切实际也没有必要的，甚至会起到事倍功半的反效果，吃力而不讨好。为了更好地贴合读者，让这本书真正为你所用，我将读者按照需求大致分为了如下三类，大家可以结合切身实际，精准地规划属于自己的自学方案。

docs.title: 初入校园
docs.text:
如果你刚刚进入大学校园或者还在低年级，并且就读的是计算机方向或者想要转到计算机方向，那么你很幸运，因为学习是你的本业，你可以有充足的时间和自由来学习自己感兴趣的东西，不会有工作的压力和生活的琐碎，不必过于纠结“学了有没有用”，“能不能找到工作”这类功利的想法。那么该如何安排大学的学习生活呢？我认为首要一点就是打破高中按部就班的学习生活方式。大学是自由的，无论是生活还是学习，尽管仍然有课堂、考试，但却并非只需刷题便能成功。首先，在大学里，你可以不局限于课本或课堂上的知识，即使在你的专业领域，你也可以扩展学习各种知识，除此以外，你更可以跨专业学习知识；其次，我希望你能少些功利心，有目标（保研、就业、出国留学等）是好事，但做事不要仅仅为了达到这些目标，更应该尽力在过程中学到能伴随你一生的知识，它们或许是学习方法、或许是一种做事方法，但少些功利心不应该成为你偷懒放纵的借口；最后，平衡好学习和生活，学习应该是生活的一部分，我本科时参加过一个社团，里面有一些近乎疯狂的人，他们甚至每天晚上在社团场地中打地铺，我不认为这是真心热爱知识的表现，相反是他们在生活上不够成熟的表现。

本书涵盖计算机领域各方面的知识，我建议你根据培养方案选择当前学年对应的课程学习，同时在课余可以选择一些课堂没有的课程加以扩展，尤其是一些使用工具和技术，例如git、docker、vue等。就目前而言，国内的计算机教学不会教授太多实践知识，而实践是本专业最重要的学习过程，所以你大概率只能靠自己动手实践，逐渐积累经验。

第一件事，是弄清楚什么叫“写得优雅”的代码。国内不少大一编程入门课容易上成枯燥的语法罗列，效果甚至不如让学生自己读官方文档。其实刚接触编程时，就去感受什么样的代码算优雅、什么样的代码“have bad taste”，是很有帮助的。入门阶段通常会先讲过程式编程，比如 C 语言，但即便是面向过程，模块化、封装这些意识也不能丢。如果写代码时只想着在 OpenJudge 上通过，图省事靠复制粘贴堆出一个庞大的 main 函数，时间一长，代码质量就很容易停在这个水平。等碰到稍微大一点的项目，调试、沟通和维护的成本会像滚雪球一样压过来。所以写的时候不妨多问自己几句：有没有大量重复？这个函数是不是承担了太多职责？Linux 的风格就是让一个函数只做好一件事。这段逻辑能不能抽成独立函数？刚开始可能会觉得别扭，甚至怀疑一道简单题何必这么折腾，但好习惯的价值是长期的。C 语言本身并不难，初中生都能学，那公司凭什么要招你来做程序员？

学过面向过程之后，大一下学期通常会转向面向对象，比如 C++ 或 Java。这里很推荐 MIT 6.031: Software Construction 的 Notes，它会以 Java（2022 年改成了 TypeScript）为例，细致讲怎么写出更优雅的代码，比如测试驱动开发、函数规格说明的设计、异常处理等。既然接触了面向对象，了解一些常见设计模式也很有必要。国内面向对象课程有时也容易变成语法课，让学生纠结继承的各种写法，甚至做类似脑筋急转弯的题目，但这些东西在真实项目里几乎用不上。面向对象真正要练的，是把实际问题抽象成若干类以及它们之间的关系；设计模式则是前人总结出来的一些抽象经验。《大话设计模式》这本书就写得比较浅显易懂，适合入门。

第二件事，是学一些能明显提升生产力的工具和技能，比如 Git、Shell、Vim。这里强烈推荐 MIT missing semester。刚上手可能很不习惯，但逼自己用一段时间，熟练后开发效率会明显上一个台阶。还有很多小工具也能提升效率。我自己的一个原则是：凡是会让手离开键盘的动作，都值得想办法省掉。切换应用、打开文件、浏览网页，都可以用插件或工具做成快捷操作，Mac 上比如 Alfred。如果一个操作每天都重复，而且每次还要花一秒以上，那就想办法把它压到 0.1 秒。毕竟以后几十年都要和电脑打交道，早点形成顺滑的工作流会省很多力。另外，盲打一定要练。如果现在还要看着键盘打字，赶紧找个教程练起来，这对开发效率帮助很大。

第三件事，是平衡好课内和自学。可以质疑现状，但规则还是要尊重，尤其绩点在保研里分量不轻。所以大一我还是建议尽量跟着课表走，同时辅以优质课外资源。比如微积分、线代可以参考 MIT 18.01/18.02 和 MIT 18.06 的课程 Notes；假期可以用 UCB CS61A 学 Python。同时把前面说的编程习惯和实践能力慢慢练起来。就个人经验看，大一数学课学分占比高，考试风格又因学校和老师差异很大。自学可能帮你理解数学本身，却不一定能换来漂亮分数。所以考前最好有针对性地做往年题，把应试这一环补上。升入大二之后，再逐步加大自学比重，可能会更稳妥。

大二以后，计算机专业的课程会逐渐多起来，这时候其实很适合把学习重心往自学上挪一挪。我把自己三年来自学的路线整理成了一份 CS 学习清单，里面简单写了每门课大概讲什么、为什么值得学。你课表上的大部分课程，基本都能在这份清单里找到对应的国外课程，而且整体质量通常更扎实。计算机专业的核心知识本来就相通，好的课程往往能把原理讲透，相比之下，不少照本宣科式的课堂就很难做到这一点。一般来说，考前把老师讲了一学期的 PPT 拿出来集中复习两天，卷面成绩通常不会太难看。如果课程有大作业，也可以把国外课程的 Lab 或 Project 拿来改一改，应付课内要求。总之，关键是要灵活：目标是更高效地掌握知识，遇到和这个目标冲突的规定，可以想办法绕开或简化处理。

最后，还是希望大家少一点浮躁和功利，多一点耐心和真正的兴趣。很多人问我，自学是不是特别需要自制力。我觉得关键还是看你自己想要什么。如果你只是觉得学会一门编程语言就能月薪过万，想赶上互联网红利，那我说再多也没用。我最初自学其实没想太多功利的东西，更多是好奇，是想弄明白一些东西。整个过程也没有想象中那么苦大仇深，该吃吃、该玩玩，回头一看，资料反而慢慢攒了不少。现在中美竞争已经是一个大背景，我们还在学习国外的高质量课程，感叹别人做得好，同时也会有一点危机感。那以后靠谁去改变呢？还是要靠刚入行的你们。所以，加油吧，少年。

docs.title: 去芜存菁
docs.text: 如果你已经本科毕业、正在读研，或者已经工作，甚至是在其他领域上班、想利用业余时间转向编程，那么你大概很难挤出足够时间，把“一份仅供参考的CS学习规划”里的内容从头到尾系统学一遍；但你又确实想补上本科阶段欠下的基础。考虑到这类读者通常已有一定编程经验，入门课程就不必再重复了。从实用角度看，工作方向大体已定，也没必要把计算机的每个分支都钻得很深，更值得投入的是那些通用性强的原则和技能。因此，我结合自己的经历，挑了几门我认为最重要、质量也最高的核心专业课，希望能帮助你更深入地理解计算机。学完这些课，不管你具体做什么工作，应该都不至于只停留在会调包的水平，而是会对计算机底层如何运行有更清楚的认识。

docs.title: 梦有所托
docs.text:
如果你对于计算机领域的核心专业课都掌握得相当扎实，而且已经确定了自己的工作或研究方向，那么书中还有很多未在 一份仅供参考的CS学习规划 提到的课程供你探索。

随着贡献者的不断增多，左侧的目录中将不断增加新的分支，例如 机器学习进阶 和 机器学习系统。并且同一个分支下都有若干同类型课程，它们有着不同的侧重点和课程实验，例如 操作系统 分支下就包含了麻省理工、伯克利、南京大学还有哈工大四所学校的课程。如果你想深耕一个领域，那么学习这些同类的课程会给你不同的视角来看待类似的知识。同时，本书作者还计划联系一些相关领域的科研工作者来分享某个细分领域的科研学习路径，让 CS自学指南 在追求广度的同时，实现深度上的提高。

如果你想贡献这方面的内容，欢迎和作者邮件联系 zhangchaowen@stu.scu.edu.cn

docs.title: 课程简介
docs.text:
• 来源：walkinglabs 开源社区课程（课程网站），非高校学分课程，以短讲形式发布
  • 先修要求：有一个真实的代码仓库、熟悉 Git 与命令行、至少用过一款编码 Agent（如 Claude Code、Codex）
  • 编程语言：不限，课程主体是仓库内的指令文件、配置与验证命令，可能涉及少量 Shell 或 Python 编写验证钩子
  • 课程难度：🌟🌟
  • 预计学时：约 12 讲，8 小时左右看课，另需至少 15 小时在自己的项目上实践

这门课讨论的是一个很朴素的问题：模型的能力强，不等于它在你的仓库里干活可靠。"harness"这个词在 AI coding agent 的圈子里被用得越来越多了，但大部分人说 harness 的时候，其实指的是一个 prompt 文件。一个 prompt 文件不是 harness。

这节课要给 harness 一个精确的、可操作的定义。不是学术论文里的抽象概念，而是你今天就能拿去用的框架。harness 由五个子系统组成：指令、工具、环境、状态、反馈。每个子系统都有明确的职责和评判标准。

Learn Harness Engineering 是一门专注于 AI 编程智能体工程化落地的课程。通过系统的环境设计、状态管理、验证与控制机制，本课程旨在帮助你让 Codex 和 Claude Code 等 AI Agent 能够真正可靠地完成真实工程任务。它通过明确的规则和边界约束你的 AI 编程助手，帮助你更可靠地构建功能、修复 Bug 并自动化开发任务。

自学的第一个坑是缺少真实项目。没有仓库可折腾时，这门课会迅速退化成概念背诵，建议挑一个自己正在维护、有一定复杂度、需要跑测试的项目作为练习场。第二个坑是过度工程：一开始就想搭出一套完美的 harness，结果配置文件越写越多、验证命令没人维护，反而增加了负担。原课程强调的“先让它可靠，再让它优雅”，从最小可用的验证回路开始更现实。第三个坑是把二手解读当成课程结论。Harness Engineering 是近年热起来的概念，译名和术语尚未统一，各类解读常有夸张成分，遇到关键论断建议回到原始讲次和 OpenAI 的 harness engineering 文章核对。

docs.title: 为什么学习 Vim或Emacs
docs.text:
Vim 和 Emacs 这两款编辑器有如下好处：

  • 让你的整个开发过程手指尽量不需要离开键盘：Vim 的模态编辑和 Emacs 的快捷键体系都把光标移动、文本操作和命令执行围绕键盘完成，避免频繁在方向键和鼠标之间切换，让手指一直处在高效输入的状态。
  • 方便的文件切换以及窗口/缓冲区管理可以让你同时开发多份文件，甚至同一个文件的不同位置：Vim 有 buffer、window、tab，Emacs 有 buffer、window、frame，都能把多任务编辑组织得很顺手。
  • Vim 的宏操作和 Emacs 的键盘宏、Elisp 脚本都可以批量化处理重复操作，例如多行缩进、批量加双引号、批量重命名等，把机械劳动交给编辑器。
  • Vim 是很多服务器自带的命令行编辑器，当你通过 ssh 连接远程服务器之后，由于没有图形界面，往往可以直接用 Vim 进行开发；Emacs 也能在终端中运行，并可借助 TRAMP 等方式远程编辑，同样适合无图形界面的环境。
  • 异常丰富的插件/扩展生态，让你拥有世界上最花里胡哨的终端编辑器组合：Vim 有海量插件，Emacs 有庞大的 Elisp 包生态，两者都能被改造成高度贴合个人工作流的开发环境。
  • 可深度定制：Vim 可以通过 vimrc、Vimscript、Lua 等配置，Emacs 可以通过 init.el 和 Elisp 配置，二者都能把编辑器打磨成个人专属工具。

docs.title: 如何学习
docs.text:
不幸的是 Vim(或Emacs) 的学习曲线确实相当陡峭，我花了好几个星期才慢慢适应了用 Vim 进行开发的过程。最开始你会觉得非常不适应，但一旦熬过了初始阶段，相信我，你会爱上它们。

Vim 和 Emacs 是两个年纪比大多数读者还大的编辑器。Vim 的前身 vi 诞生于 1976 年的伯克利，Emacs 的雏形在 MIT 的 AI 实验室出现得更早，Richard Stallman 后来把它整理成 GNU Emacs。它们活到今天并不是靠怀旧，而是因为它们在一个几乎所有编辑器都放弃的方向上坚持的足够久：把编辑这件事拆成最小的、可以用键盘组合的原子操作，然后允许用户自己组装。

Vim 的答案是把编辑分成“模式”。在普通模式里，按键不是用来输入字符，而是动作：d 是删除操作符，w 是文本对象“下一个词”，合起来 dw 就是删一个词，ci" 是“改变引号里的内容”。这套组合语法的好处是可以无限派生，一旦熟悉，编辑就从逐字移动变成对结构的一次性操作。代价是学习曲线陡峭，前两周的效率会明显下降。

Emacs 的答案不是模式，而是一个可编程的运行环境。它本质上是一台 Lisp 解释器，编辑器只是它的第一个应用，所以按键绑定的枚举、缓冲区（buffer）、窗口（window）乃至邮件、日程、终端都统一在这一套抽象下。这种“编辑器即操作系统”的路线让 Emacs 的可定制性几乎没有上限，org-mode 就是在这个文化里长出来的：一个纯文本的标记格式，却能承担笔记、待办、日程、表格运算和代码块执行。

两者都不是轻松的选择。本篇的价值不在于说服你换编辑器，而在于提供一个有顺序的学习路径，让你能在真实项目里边用边学，而不是卡在配置阶段。学习时最重要的一条原则是：先会用，再会配。Vim 的多数插件只是对自带功能的封装，Emacs 的多数发行版（如 Doom、Spacemacs、Centaur）把别人的配置打包给你，直接套用会让你在出问题时完全无从下手。

• 来源：Learn Git Branching 开源互动教程（课程网站），以浏览器内可视化沙盒的形式发布
  • 先修要求：无需任何 Git 或图形化客户端经验；能使用命令行（知道 cd、ls 等基础命令）即可，了解“版本控制”大致是用来保存历史版本的即可
  • 课程难度：🌟
  • 预计学时：主线与远程仓库两部分约 8 小时，全部通读并完成挑战关约 15 小时

它把 Git 的分支操作变成可玩的关卡。教程围绕几个核心关卡组展开：基础篇讲 commit、branch、merge、rebase，进阶篇讲在提交之间移动的 checkout、reset、revert、cherry-pick 与交互式 rebase，然后是“移动提交记录”“杂项”“高级话题”等组，最后是远程仓库部分，覆盖 clone、fetch、pull、push、跟踪分支与远程分支。每个关卡只有一个明确目标，右侧是可视化仓库图，你输入命令后提交节点与分支指针会立即移动，目标达成即通关，进度保存在浏览器本地。

它最大的优势是把抽象的分支模型直接变成图像。Git 最令人困惑的地方在于“提交是节点、分支是指针、HEAD 是当前位置”这套心智模型，讲义里写十遍也不如亲手用 git rebase 把游离的提交贴到另一条分支上、看着节点在图中重排来得直观。其次，每一个关卡都是先演示再练习，左侧有简短说明与命令提示，右侧随时可以用 undo 和 reset 撤销，失败零成本，因此可以放心大胆地试错，这在真实仓库里不可能做到。相较于《Pro Git》这类系统教材，它不逐项讲解原理与配置；相较于零散的 Git 速查表，它又提供了循序渐进的顺序和即时反馈。

来源：LaTeX 官方项目与 CTEX 社区中文资料综合整理（LaTeX 项目）

LaTeX 是基于 TeX 的排版系统，TeX 由 Knuth 开发，LaTeX 由 Lamport 在其上封装，两位都是计算机领域举足轻重的人物。不过开发者厉害并不是我们要学它的理由。它和 Word 这类所见即所得的软件最大的区别是分工：你只负责写内容，排版交给系统自动完成。标题层级、图表编号、公式间距、参考文献格式，全都由样式规则统一决定，因此没有任何排版经验的人也能写出排版专业的文章。

这个特点在长文档上体现得最明显。论文写到一百页时，手动调格式的代价会呈指数上升，而 LaTeX 只要开头把样式定义好，后面新增的每一节都会自动遵循同一套规则，编号与目录也会自动更新。数学公式更是它的传统强项，复杂的分式、矩阵、多重下标写起来比任何图形界面都自然。

学习路径相对清晰，难点主要在起步。环境配置是第一个拦路虎，本地装 TeX 发行版经常遇到缺宏包与字体问题，用 Overleaf这样的在线编辑器可以跳过这一步，站内还有大量现成模板可以直接改。

• 来源：Scoop 官方文档与社区实践整理（Scoop 官网）
  • 先修要求：熟悉 Windows 下的 PowerShell 基本操作，了解什么是环境变量
  • 课程难度：🌟

Windows 下搭建开发环境一直是个麻烦事。没有统一标准，每个工具的安装方式都不一样，有的要下载安装包点下一步，有的要解压后手动配环境变量，装十个工具就能耗掉一整天。Scoop 的作用是把这些差异统一掉：它把常见的命令行工具集中管理起来，安装与升级一条命令完成，环境变量也自动处理。

上手极简单，装 Python 与 Node.js 就是两行：

scoop install python
scoop install nodejs

安装 Scoop 本身需要 PowerShell 5.1 及以上。Windows 10 及以后版本自带，Windows 7 自带的版本太旧，需要先手动升级。这里有个国内用户常踩的细节：不少人设置 Windows 用户时用了中文用户名，用户目录随之变成中文路径，而 Scoop 默认把软件装在用户目录下，部分软件在中文路径下会执行出错。建议用 -ScoopDir 参数装到纯英文的自定义目录：

Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser
irm get.scoop.sh -outfile 'install.ps1'
.\install.ps1 -ScoopDir 'C:\Scoop'

它最大的好处是把“装软件”变成可重复、可迁移的动作。换一台机器时，把安装清单重新执行一遍就能恢复环境，不用回忆当年每一个安装包的选项。

docs.title: 课程简介
docs.text:
• 来源：davidkimai 发起的开源课程 Context-Engineering（课程网站），原始内容托管在 GitHub 仓库
  • 先修要求：熟悉提示工程基础（零样本、少样本、链式思考），会写 Python 并调用过至少一种 LLM API；涉及记忆、RAG、Agent 的章节需要理解向量检索与工具调用的基本概念
  • 编程语言：Python，讲义中的示例以 Notebook 风格的单文件脚本提供，配置文件使用 YAML
  • 课程难度：🌟🌟🌟🌟
  • 预计学时：课程自述为 12 周的分阶段学习路径，按每周 4 至 6 小时估算约 50 至 70 小时；若只读基础与系统实现两部分，20 小时左右可完成第一遍

课程的核心命题是：提示工程只解决“你说什么”，上下文工程解决“模型看到的其他一切”。作者引用 Karpathy 的定义——上下文工程是“把刚刚好的信息填进上下文窗口的细腻艺术”，并采用 A Survey of Context Engineering（综述 1400 余篇论文）的界定：上下文不只是用户发出去的那段提示词，而是推理时刻提供给模型的完整信息载荷，涵盖示例、记忆、检索结果、工具、状态与控制流。课程用一套生物学隐喻搭起递进的四级结构：原子（单条指令与简单约束）、分子（少样本示例与演示集）、细胞（持久记忆、状态管理、上下文窗口）、器官（多步流程、专家分工、系统编排），之上是神经系统与语义场（推理框架、验证工具、认知模式、吸引子与共振），再到协议壳与统一系统，最后是元递归框架（自我反思、递归改进、可解释演化）。每个层级都对应现实中的技术形态，从基础提示工程一路映射到多 Agent 系统与自组织系统。

相较同类材料，它最鲜明的特点是把上下文当成一个可以“度量、删减、编排”的工程对象，而不是一堆提示技巧的集合。课程给出六条明确的方法论：从第一性原理出发、只补模型确实缺失的部分、对 token 成本与延迟与质量分数全部量化、删除优于堆砌、代码优于幻灯片（每个概念都有可运行单元）、一切都要可视化（ASCII 图与符号图贯穿全篇）。同时它把最新研究直接嵌进教材，例如 MEM1 的记忆与推理合并、IBM Zurich 的认知工具（把结构化提示模板当工具调用，使 GPT-4.1 在 AIME2024 上 pass@1 从 26.7% 提升到 43.3%）、ICML Princeton 关于涌现符号机制的三段式注意力结构，这些论文被用来解释为什么 Markdown、JSON 这类结构化格式更利于模型解析。

• 来源：DAIR.AI 发起的开源项目 Prompt Engineering Guide（中文站点、英文站点），以在线文档形式持续更新，配套维护 GitHub 仓库
  • 先修要求：无需机器学习背景，能正常使用任意一款大语言模型（ChatGPT、Claude、Gemini、Kimi、DeepSeek 等）即可入门；读“模型”“研究论文”部分时，具备 Transformer 与注意力机制的基本认识会更顺畅
  • 课程难度：🌟🌟
  • 预计学时：通读约 20 小时，配合动手实验（在每个技术章节自己复现一遍提示）建议 40 小时以上

课程的核心优势是“概念—示例—论文”三位一体。同一个技术先给一句直觉解释，再给出可直接复制的提示词，然后贴出原始论文的实验设置与结果，让人知道这个技巧为什么有效、在什么条件下会失效。相较于零散的博客与短视频，它成体系、有出处、有实验支撑；相较于直接去读论文，它先把术语和动机铺平，阅读门槛低了很多。中英双站内容基本对齐，中文站对大部分技术章节做了翻译，专业名词保留英文括注，便于对照原始文献。

前十来页几乎不需要任何背景知识，半小时就能上手改自己的提示词，成就感来得很直接；越往后越偏研究导向，尤其是思维树、自我一致性、Directional Stimulus Prompting 这类方法，会引用较多论文结论，不习惯读实验表格的话容易卡在细节里。建议把它当成一份“可查阅的路线图”而不是一本线性教材，第一遍通读抓框架，遇到具体任务再回来查对应章节。

docs.title: 课程简介
docs.text:
• 来源：《Hello 算法》开源教程（课程网站），作者靳宇栋（Krahets），以开源电子书形式发布
  • 先修要求：掌握任意一门编程语言的基本语法（变量、循环、函数、递归），对数组和链表有直观认识即可
  • 编程语言：示例覆盖 Java、C++、Python、Go、JavaScript、TypeScript、C#、Rust、Swift、Dart、Zig 等十余种语言，同一段逻辑提供多语言版本
  • 课程难度：🌟🌟
  • 预计学时：通读约 40 小时，配合动手实现与刷题建议 60 小时以上

全书分复杂度分析、数据结构、算法三个大模块。数据结构部分讲数组与链表、栈与队列、哈希表、二叉树、堆、图，算法部分讲搜索、排序、分治、回溯、动态规划与贪心。每章按“定义、实现、应用场景”的顺序展开，先给知识地图，再逐个结构拆解，最后用算法范式收束，适合作为数据结构与算法的第一本书。

它最突出的特点是动画图解与可运行代码。每个关键操作都有逐帧动画，把数据在内存中的变化过程演给你看，比静态配图更容易建立直觉；所有示例代码可以直接运行，注释详细，并且同一段逻辑给出了十多种语言的实现，方便用自己熟悉的语言对照阅读。相较于《算法导论》这类偏理论与证明的教材，它更像一张能边走边动手的路线图；相较于各类刷题笔记，它成体系、有取舍，不会一上来就堆技巧。

学习曲线确实平滑：章节短、图多、文字少，一天翻一章不容易卡住，对零基础读者非常友好。但也要清楚它的定位是入门，进阶结构如红黑树、B 树、并查集、线段树没有展开，复杂度分析的数学推导偏浅，动态规划也只覆盖经典模型。读完能看懂大部分题解，却不足以直接应付竞赛或大厂算法面试的难题，后续还需要另一门更硬的课程接续。

自学的第一个坑是把“看懂动画”当成“掌握了”。动画直观到会产生错觉，真正动手时才会发现边界条件、数组下标、递归终止条件一个都不能少，建议每看完一节就合上书自己实现一遍。第二个坑是缺少配套练习。这本书讲原理，不提供足量题目，不刷题很难形成手感，建议同步用 LeetCode 按专题补题。第三个坑是多语言示例带来的干扰。入门阶段请盯住一门语言看，别在多语言之间来回对照，否则注意力会跑到语法差异上，而不是算法本身。

  • 预计学时：体系化通读基础与进阶两部分约 80 小时，按专题深入并配合选题练习建议 150 小时以上

OI Wiki 是一个面向信息学奥林匹克竞赛（OI）的知识库，不按学期授课，而是以百科条目组织知识点。内容大致分为三块：一是基础部分，涵盖语言基础、复杂度分析、枚举、模拟、递归、贪心、二分、搜索、动态规划入门与字符串基础；二是搜索、动态规划、图论、数据结构、字符串几大专题的进阶版本，包括状态压缩 DP、树形 DP、斜率优化、并查集、树状数组、线段树、平衡树、图论建模、网络流与各类字符串算法；三是数学与竞赛技巧，如数论、组合数学、线性代数、多项式、博弈论，以及数据结构与算法在具体题目中的综合运用。

它最大的特点是完整而深。像可持久化线段树、Link-Cut Tree、动态树、Min_25 筛这类在教材里几乎不会出现、竞赛中却反复考的内容，这里都有独立条目，并配有推导、模板代码与例题链接，覆盖范围从入门一直延伸到省队以上水平。每条目通常先给定义与朴素思路，再推优化，最后给复杂度与代码模板，还带页脚参考资料，便于沿着引用继续读原始论文与博客。

自学的第一个坑是不做前置筛选就硬啃进阶条目。线段树与平衡树都默认你熟悉递归、树结构与指针操作，直接跳进去读模板只会背下代码却不懂原理，请先把基础部分与递归、二分、并查集吃透。第二个坑是把模板当答案。OI Wiki 的代码模板通常并不是该问题的最优写法，直接抄写会错过设计思路，也无法在变形题上迁移，每个模板都应当自己再实现一遍并改掉变量命名去理解细节。第三个坑是忽略数学专题。数论、组合数学与矩阵快速幂往往是竞赛题的分水岭，而它们读起来最枯燥；建议在遇到具体题型时反查，而不是从头排开去阅读，否则很容易半途放弃。

docs.title: Easy RL 强化学习教程
课程简介
docs.text:
• 来源：Datawhale 开源社区教程《Easy RL：强化学习教程》（俗称“蘑菇书”，课程网站），作者王琦、杨毅远、江季，已由人民邮电出版社出版纸质版
  • 先修要求：熟练使用 Python，了解概率论（随机变量、期望、条件概率）、线性代数与微积分基础，并具备深度学习常识（神经网络、反向传播、梯度下降）
  • 编程语言：Python，代码主要基于 PyTorch 与 Gym
  • 课程难度：🌟🌟🌟
  • 预计学时：通读约 60 小时，配合跑通算法代码与做习题建议 100 小时以上

课程内容分两大部分。第一部分（第 1 至 3 章）打基础，从强化学习与其他机器学习范式的区别讲起，接着是马尔可夫决策过程（MP、MRP、MDP 的层层递进）与表格型方法（Q 表、Sarsa、Q-learning、策略评估与改进）。第二部分（第 4 至 13 章）进入深度强化学习，覆盖免模型预测与控制、深度学习基础、DQN 及其变体、针对连续动作的 DQN、策略梯度、Actor-Critic、DDPG、PPO，以及稀疏奖励、模仿学习等实战问题的处理方法。第二部分各章相对独立，可以按兴趣选读，这为不同目标的读者留出了自由度。

它的核心优势在于中文、成体系、有习题。这本书最初是对李宏毅《深度强化学习》公开课以及周博磊、David Silver 等讲义的整理与再组织，把视频里跳跃性较强的内容补成完整推导，每章末尾附有习题与解答，读起来不像论文综述那样零散。相较于 Sutton 的《强化学习》那种以理论为主、公式密度极高的原典，它更偏工程实现与直觉建立；相较于各类开源 RL 代码库，它不跳步，把每个算法为什么这样设计讲清楚了。业界的说法是这本书“读得下去”，我认为主要得益于它保留了公式推导但配以大量图示与中文解释。

体验上可以感受到明显的陡峭感。前三章读起来轻松，但一到 DQN 部分，目标网络、经验回放、时序差分、重要性采样这些概念会集中涌来，如果深度学习基础不牢，容易在此时掉队。建议在第二部分开始前先复习一遍神经网络训练与梯度下降，把“为什么需要目标网络”这类动机问题想明白，比硬记公式有效得多。

自学的第一个坑是只读不跑。强化学习的很多细节只有跑通代码才能暴露，比如奖励尺度、探索率衰减、采样效率，光看书会觉得已经懂了，实际训练不收敛时才知道问题在哪，建议把每章的 Q-learning、DQN、PPO 至少各跑通一个环境。第二个坑是跳过第一部分直奔深度强化学习。MDP、贝尔曼方程、时序差分是整个学科的共同语言，不扎实就会在后面反复卡壳。第三个坑是对数学符号的畏难。书里的推导确实需要一点耐心，但绝大多数步骤都是期望与梯度的基本操作，遇到卡住的地方回看前两章，或者对照李宏毅的公开课视频，往往一句话就通了。最后提醒一句，这本书写于较早日，部分库版本与代码接口已有变化，跑代码时以官方仓库的最新分支为准。

docs.title: 自我革新
docs.text: 结合我本人对自我与外在事物的思考，以及对生活的感悟，我在这里简单提及一些我的生活。如果你不感兴趣可以完全跳过，这只是一个题外专栏。另外如果你也想分享自己的人生经历，欢迎通过邮箱 zhangchaowen@stu.scu.edu.cn联系我。

docs.title: 阅读
docs.text:
世界上任何书籍都不能带给你好运，但它们能让你悄悄成为你自己。

阅读我上了大学后才喜欢的爱好，再此之前，我自认为是一个无比普通平凡的人。刚入大学时，一个同乡的学长给我推荐了一些哲学的书籍，我闲来无事便找了电子书来看看，我发现其实读书也没有那么枯燥，随着作者的思想经历各式各样的思想之旅反而是很有趣的。当然，让我真正坚持并热爱读书还是因为我自身的问题。一方面，我需要阅读一些书籍来入门计算机专业，我还记得当时看的是啊哈 C学的C语言；另一方面，上大学后，我很想脱离高中时期的循规守矩，想了解各个专业的知识。我原本是一个非常内向的男孩，我不喜欢上课回答问题，汇报ppt，因为我有改变的原因和动力，我阅读了《被讨厌的勇气》，它让我找到了很大的面对生活的勇气，也让我如今能够不再惧怕失去所谓的面子，活出了真正的自我。同时，因为自我成长的规划，我还阅读过经济学、哲学、文学、天文学、物理学、生物学、语言学等方面的书籍，尽管我对一些领域不感兴趣，例如文学，我很少看这些领域的书籍，但是偶尔找到一本适合自己的也能读完，不过我并不会强迫自己阅读不感兴趣的书籍。

阅读对我最大的好处并非是知识，尽管它们在我的工作生活中很重要，但最重要的是他们重塑了我的世界观和思想。世界上任何书籍都不能带给你好运，但它们能让你悄悄成为你自己。如果你非要问一个阅读的好处，我觉得对于每个人最大的好处应该是，让你活出自我。人是群居生物，我不喜欢平庸，大事上我很少从众。人天生有从众的趋势，从众当然不是坏事，但久而久之，你的判断力越来越大众化--平凡，如果你再想活出自我的理想，便会难如登天，因为人一旦从事理想，便会遇到困难，大部分人会劝你放弃，而你长期从众而失去判断力，理想便会归于平淡。不过老实说，平凡并非坏事，这个世界大部分人都是普通人，不过总的来说，书籍带来的知识和思想，仍然是我们宝贵的财富。

最后一句话先给你，我们读书是因为，如果我们身边都是平凡而不出众的人，那么我们从小形成的世界观和思想也平平无奇。但是我们通过阅读天才们的书，能够学到他们超越常人的思想，从而应用到生活中，至少我们能真正活出自我的意愿。

docs.title: 终身学习
docs.text:
人生两大不幸：毕业后不再学习，结婚后不再恋爱

终身学习的思想存在了上千年，但却是极少人能做到的。尤其是对于计算机行业的人而言，终身学习可谓最重要的准则。计算机领域发展极快，短短几十年，便从每秒仅能运算数千次的电子管巨兽，发展到算力亿万倍于它、无处不在的智能设备。能做到终身学习是很难的，这不仅仅靠你了解其思想，更重要的是将其融入你的个性中。如果你在生活中能做到无意识的持续学习，那你或许已掌握终身学习的诀窍了。

docs.title: 习惯即一切
docs.text:
卓越不是单一的举动，而是习惯。

人类做事，大部分其实靠习惯。每天睡懒觉是习惯，早起运动是习惯，定期打扫卫生是习惯，随意扔袜子也是习惯。习惯可以减少我们的思考，从而让我们保持精力充沛。如果你想改善自己，例如每天早睡早起，每天坚持锻炼，你都需要养成一个好习惯。可养成习惯哪有那么容易，以我自己的经历来看，如果我能坚持一个事情一周，我大概率可以养成这个习惯，当然不同习惯形成周期略有波动。我个人养成习惯很简单，如果我想到一件事，例如我想提升认知、亦或是我想完美身材，我就想出一种解决方式，例如读书和锻炼，我会给自己灌输一种思想，如果一件事对我有利，我就应该爱上它，再此之前，我会装作爱上它。毕竟如果你模仿疯子在大街上裸奔，实际上你就是疯子；如果你模仿智者，实际上你就是智者。最后，我会在开始时简单做这件事，例如锻炼10分钟即可（尽管这可能没有效果），再慢慢形成习惯后，逐步加强。甚至一开始你可以只是下楼去健身房即可，一旦你去了，你潜意识也会告诉你来都来了。相信我，慢慢的，你会变得更加优秀的。不过，一开始不要同时养成太多习惯，人的精力是有限的。

docs.title: Foreword
docs.text:
This book is an open-source, free guide to a computer science curriculum for the AI era. It is a gift to the juniors who come after me, and my small contribution to the open-source community.

If this guide helps you even a little, that will be encouragement and comfort enough for me.

The book currently contains the following parts (if you have better ideas, or would like to join the contributors, feel free to reach me at zhangchaowen@stu.scu.edu.cn, or open an Issue):

  • How to Use This Guide: the book covers a great many resources, so I have written usage guides for readers with different amounts of free time and different learning goals.
  • AICS Learning Plan: a learning plan for the AI era of computer science, for reference only.

docs.title: Where the Journey Began
docs.text:
When I entered university I was a complete beginner in computing. Apart from playing PC games, I could not even install legitimate software. Still, I began my computer science journey with curiosity and enthusiasm. Every day I went to class on time, listened attentively to the lectures, took careful notes, and completed the assignments. Yet I gradually realized that every teacher taught differently, at a different pace, with different emphases and different levels of enthusiasm. Some merely read out an outdated slide deck; some did little more than call on students to answer questions already printed on the slides. Very few were genuinely committed to teaching and to making students think critically. Day after day of this dull routine wore my enthusiasm down... I lost my bearings, and for a while I wondered whether computer science was simply not for me, because everything I had imagined about geeks as a child had been shattered by my first year. I kept asking myself: if AI can do so many things, what do I actually need to learn? Do I still need to learn Java and Python? Do I still need data structures and computer networks? I assumed my university years would pass quietly like this: classes, studying, entertainment. Then, within a couple of months, DeepSeek-V3 arrived on the scene, and everyone around me was raving about this brand-new model.

As a beginner, I thought it was no big deal — just one more tool to help me write code. I went on grinding through the four core courses in their conventional order, just as before, until near the start of my second year, when my data structures teacher happened to share a post in the group chat: the text of Andrew Ng's talk at a Buildathon. The moment I saw it I was hooked. I read the whole thing in one sitting, and still unsatisfied, went to YouTube to watch the original video.

The talk was about AI-assisted programming, rapid prototyping, and the skills an AI engineer needs. For the first time I saw clearly where this industry — and every industry — is heading: understand AI and master AI.

From Andrew Ng's talk I drew several key ideas:

  • "Move fast and take responsibility." AI-assisted programming brings a tenfold speed-up to solo prototype development. When the cost of a prototype falls dramatically, rapid and repeated trial and error becomes a viable strategy, and the real value lies in discovering, through that trial and error, the projects worth developing seriously.

  • Code is depreciating, and developers must become system designers and AI conductors. Programming tools have already gone through several generations: from GitHub Copilot to IDE integration to highly agentic coding assistants. Tools iterate fast enough to create real gaps in productivity, and falling half a generation behind can significantly limit your output. The value of code itself is declining. AI can generate code and migrate database schemas automatically, which makes architectural decisions far more reversible. Developers must shift from writing code to designing systems and conducting AI, focusing on core architecture and building composite systems.

  • "You don't need to learn programming in the AI era" is the worst career advice ever given. Andrew Ng strongly rejects this idea, pointing out that every advance in programming tools in history has enabled more people to program. His team's CFO, legal counsel and receptionist all learned to program and improved their productivity as a result. The core skill of the future is "telling the computer precisely what to do," which requires understanding computer languages and programming logic. Non-technical people can acquire basic programming ability quickly with AI assistance and boost their efficiency across domains.

  • AI engineers are scarce, yet university curricula are badly out of date. The unemployment rate for computer science graduates has risen to 7%, while companies still face a severe shortage of AI engineers. The core contradiction is that university courses fail to cover the key skills in time: AI-assisted programming, LLM API usage, building RAG and agentic workflows, and structured error analysis. The emerging AI engineer needs three capabilities: proficiency with the latest AI coding tools, familiarity with AI building blocks (prompt engineering, evaluation techniques, MCP), and the ability to prototype quickly with basic product intuition.

After that, I began teaching myself along the directions Andrew Ng suggested. I gradually drifted away from university lectures and found many high-quality course resources in the process. With courses like these, you have nothing to worry about: effort, seriousness and time are all it takes. The frustration I had felt in class — having energy but nowhere to put it, putting in endless hours with no return — vanished. This suited me perfectly, and I fell in love with self-directed learning.

If you too are struggling with computer science and share my confusion, take a look at Professor Ng's Buildathon talk, because that is where my heart was first set on this path.

docs.title: Why This Book
docs.text:
While studying operating systems in the autumn of my second year, I found the lectures dreadfully dull: many examples were ten years old, and the lab guide dated back thirteen years. Talking with friends, I could also feel everyone's worry about the rapid rise of AI and anxiety about future employment. By then I had been self-studying for over a year and had collected a lot of resources, so I shared them with my friends — after all, who would not want to enjoy university life, land a good job, or get into graduate school?

After another year of accumulation, the resources had grown substantial, covering most courses in computer science, intelligence and software engineering programs. I also set up a separate GitHub repository for each course, collecting study materials and my own assignment solutions. Later, while counting credits, I opened my own degree plan and found that it had become a subset of my self-study repository — only two years after I started. Then a bold idea took shape: perhaps I could build a self-study curriculum, recording the pitfalls and paths I had met over three years of self-teaching, combining them with my thinking about the AI era, and offering something small to the CS students who come after me.

docs.title: Self-Study or Not?
docs.text:
The greatest benefit of self-study is that you can adjust your pace entirely according to your own progress. You can change your plan at any time and go at your own speed, instead of being constrained by a degree plan and a classroom.

Another benefit is drawing on the best of many sources. The first time I installed a dual-boot system on my laptop I made a mistake and wiped Windows. The only saving grace was that I had no precious data at the time. Later I learned that modern SSDs do not erase data permanently: as long as the new system has not occupied that part of the disk, the data may still be recoverable. It was precisely through such mistakes that I kept learning things I would never have encountered otherwise.

A third benefit is freedom over your time. University life is already relatively free, and self-study frees you further to arrange your own schedule and plan. With sensible time management, you can study independently and still get good grades.

Are there downsides? Of course — every rose has its thorn.

The first is that it is hard to ask for help. The problem you run into may be one nobody else has hit, or nobody cares about. Still, asking well on Google, StackOverflow and AI platforms can solve 90% of your problems. The second is that many excellent courses and resources are in English, but that is no longer a serious obstacle, since translation tools and browser extensions now handle it almost perfectly. The third, and by far the hardest, is self-discipline. Having no deadlines is a truly frightening situation. As the material deepens, the difficulty rises, and finishing an entire course is a punishing grind. You need enough drive to force yourself to sit down, understand thousand-line codebases, and endure hours of debugging. And all of it comes with no credit, no GPA, no teacher, no classmates — only one conviction: you are getting stronger.

docs.title: Who This Book Is For
docs.text: Anyone who is motivated to learn and use computer science well can consult this book. If you already have some foundation and are only interested in one particular field, pick the parts that interest you. And if you, like me back then, know nothing about computing and have just entered university, I hope this book can serve as your walkthrough, so that you spend the least time acquiring the knowledge and skills you need. In a sense, this book is more like a course search engine ordered by my own experience, helping you sample excellent computer science courses without leaving home.

docs.title: Special Thanks
docs.text: Here I would like to sincerely thank, with great respect, all the professors and developers who have open-sourced their course materials for free. Those courses and resources embody decades of accumulated teaching experience and dedication, and their authors chose selflessly to let everyone enjoy such high-quality CS education. Without them, my university life would not have been so full and joyful. Many professors even replied with long emails of hundreds of words after receiving my thank-you notes, which moved me deeply. They remind me constantly: whatever you do — studying, research, or simply being a decent person — do it with your whole heart.

docs.title: Join the Contributors
docs.text: One person's strength is ultimately limited. I wrote this book late at night in the gaps of a heavy research schedule, so it is bound to have imperfections. Moreover, since my own work is in applied computing, many of the courses emphasize hands-on practice and cover relatively little mathematics, theoretical computer science, or advanced algorithms. If you have rich self-study experience and resources in other fields, you are welcome to open a Pull Request in the project, or contact me by email (zhangchaowen@stu.scu.edu.cn).

docs.title: Discussion Groups
docs.text: This book supports comments on its pages. If you want to study a course together with others, you can set up a group chat (QQ or WeChat both work), then leave a comment under the corresponding course page stating your learning goal and how to join. Besides, quite a few readers have already set up groups in Issues, which you can join directly.

docs.title: Buy the Author a Cup of Tea
docs.text: The content of this book is entirely open-source and free. If you find this project helpful, you can star the repository, or buy the author a cup of afternoon tea.

docs.title: A Learning Plan for Reference Only
docs.text:
This guide aims to build a computer science learning system for the AI era: to help beginners in computing establish a systematic knowledge structure, master modern software engineering and AI application development, and find a professional direction that suits them.

This guide does not require every learner to complete all the courses in a fixed order. You can choose the path that suits your own foundation, stage of study and goals.

docs.title: Tools and Skills
docs.text:
“Give me six hours to chop down a tree and I will spend the first four sharpening the axe.”

Tools and skills are rarely taught in school, yet they are essential for working and studying efficiently.

Tool or skill Description Learning to ask Learning to ask. If you have just entered this field, you may not even know how to ask a question properly. When you hit a problem, first ask AI, then use a search engine, and only as a last resort bother other people. I recommend reading How To Ask Questions The Smart Way to learn what a real question looks like. Magic (bypassing the firewall) For reasons everyone knows, sites such as Google and GitHub are inaccessible from the mainland, which also cuts us off from some resources we need. At such times a little magic (network circumvention) comes in handy. shell The command line (shell) is an overlooked skill, but in practice it greatly increases your flexibility and productivity as an engineer. The Art of Command Line is a classic tutorial, and I strongly recommend that you master some basic shell commands. Development environment and editor A development environment is a programmer's basic workplace. If you are a Mac user you are in luck: this guide will walk you through setting up an entire development environment step by step. If you are a Windows user, thanks to the open-source community you can enjoy a similar experience with Scoop. Nowadays we mostly use integrated environments such as Visual Studio; the most famous of these is VS Code, where a range of extensions lets you configure a good environment and boost your efficiency. Development toolchains for programming languages Compilers, package managers, dependency and build tools. Modern IDEs are powerful enough to build and run code with one click, but in some cases (to understand how a build works, or to squeeze out the last drop of build performance) you still need the toolchain, such as GNU Make. Making good use of GNU Make will build the habit of modular code and familiarize you with how large projects are compiled and linked. Git Version control, branch merging, PRs and collaborative workflows. A source control tool, and certainly one of the indispensable skills for every CS student. Markdown Writing READMEs, notes and technical documents. The most widely used document format in the computing industry; once you learn it, you gain the power to lay out documents with finesse. Docker Containerized development environments and image deployment. A lighter-weight tool than virtual machines for packaging software and deploying environments. Vim/Emacs Efficient terminal editors and remote development. Vim is a command-line editor that greatly boosts your development speed; Emacs is its equally famous rival, with comparable efficiency and much greater extensibility. Latex Academic papers and standardized document typesetting. A touch of class A typesetting tool for papers.

docs.title: Fundamentals of Computer Science
docs.text:
“A house is built from the ground up.”

The fundamentals of computer science are the shared foundation of all higher-level abilities, and the part AI finds hardest to fill in for you. Code can be generated, but understanding of principles cannot be outsourced: when you meet a performance bottleneck, a bizarre concurrency bug, or a production outage, what saves you is precisely those “old” subjects — operating systems, networks, data structures. Start broad and then go deep; every course below comes with classic courses and textbooks for its field. You do not need to finish them all, just walk one path through that suits you.

Course Description Mathematical foundations Calculus, linear algebra, discrete mathematics. Mathematics decides how far you can go in this profession: calculus is the gateway to understanding gradients and optimization, linear algebra is the language of all machine learning and graphics, and discrete mathematics is the common bedrock of algorithms, cryptography and compiler theory. Learn calculus and linear algebra to the point where they are “carved into your bones” in your first year, rather than forgetting them right after the exam. If the lectures are opaque, consult MIT 18.06 and the beautiful animated videos of 3Blue1Brown that reveal the essence of mathematics. Programming fundamentals C/C++, Java, Python. Programming languages are tools; what matters is understanding the design ideas behind them: arrays, strings, pointers, object orientation. Beginners should not study several languages at once. Go deep into one first, then use a second to understand a different paradigm and ecosystem — that will take you further than “a little of everything.” Data structures and algorithms Algorithms are the heart of computer science, unavoidable in interviews and coding practice, and the foundation of almost every professional course. The eternal theme of an algorithms course is how to turn a real problem into an algorithmic one through mathematical abstraction, then solve it with suitable data structures under constraints of time and memory. Beginners can start with Hello Algo to build intuition; see ALGO-101: Hello Algo. Digital logic and computer organization Logic circuits, CPUs, instructions and the memory hierarchy. This block answers a simple question: how does a program actually run? To build that understanding in a way that is both fun and complete, I highly recommend Nand2Tetris, which builds a computer from scratch, followed by an architecture course such as UCB CS61C. Operating systems The operating system virtualizes messy, complicated hardware into an elegant set of abstractions and is the shared foundation of every application. The real gain from this course usually comes from doing, and nothing deepens understanding like writing a kernel yourself: I recommend MIT 6.S081 (based on xv6) and this repository. Computer networks The renowned Stanford CS144: Computer Networks, whose eight projects take you through implementing the entire TCP/IP stack. If you only want a theoretical grasp of networks, read the textbook accompanying UCB CS168, available here. Database systems CMU's legendary CMU 15-445: Introduction to Database Systems uses four projects to add features to bustub, a relational database built for teaching. The grading framework is open-sourced for free, which makes it ideal for self-study. The projects also use many C++11 features, making it a good chance to sharpen your C++ skills. Compilers and programming languages For theory, read the famous “Dragon Book.” Hands-on practice is the best way to master compilers, so I recommend the Peking University compiler practice course, whose rich labs and step-by-step documentation guide you in writing a compiler from a C-like language to RISC-V assembly. There are many other high-quality labs in the compiler course directory as well. Software engineering There is a fundamental difference between code that “runs” and high-quality industrial code. I recommend Berkeley's UCB CS169: Software Engineering. Be warned, however: unlike the software engineering courses at most schools, this one does not follow the traditional design-and-document model, which emphasizes class diagrams, flowcharts and document design. Instead it adopts the Agile Development model of rapid iteration in small teams, and the Software as a Service model built on cloud platforms. Theory of computation and foundations of AI Computability, complexity, and the foundations of AI and machine learning. This part is theoretical, but what it gives you is a sense of limits: which problems are fundamentally unsolvable, which are solvable but at unacceptable cost, and why some optimizations are doomed to be futile. It is also the starting point for understanding modern AI, helping you see the relationships and differences among traditional AI, machine learning and deep learning — and avoid remembering only the names of tools amid a technological boom while being unable to say what they solve.

docs.title: Engineering Skills for the AI Era
docs.text:
“Standing on the shoulders of giants.”

This section differs most from a conventional curriculum, but that does not mean you can skip the fundamentals. It has two tracks: one uses AI to speed up work — writing code, debugging and reading source code all get faster; the other uses AI to build things — combining models, retrieval and tool calling into usable applications. Anyone can write a prompt; the hard part is making a system stable, evaluable, monitorable and cost-controlled.

Course Description Fundamentals of AI and LLMs How models work, tokens, embeddings, and the limits of their abilities. I recommend Karpathy's Neural Networks: Zero to Hero to hand-write GPT from scratch, and Dive into Deep Learning. Prompt engineering Instruction design, structured output, tool calling and prompt evaluation. Read The Prompt Engineering Guide, then compare results on a batch of test samples. AI-assisted learning Using AI to read textbooks, source code and papers, with independent verification. Let AI explain, push back with counterexamples, and verify by hand — and avoid the illusion of “I think I understand it.” AI-assisted software development AI coding tools, agent-driven software development, and engineering practice. Start with Claude Code, Codex and DeepSeek Harness. AI-assisted software engineering Requirements, design, testing, review, migration and CI/CD. Put AI into the whole software lifecycle, not just the typing stage. Building LLM applications LLM APIs, streaming output, structured responses, RAG and agent applications. To begin, follow Anthropic's courses and run the examples line by line. Retrieval-augmented generation and knowledge engineering Document splitting, retrieval, reranking, RAG evaluation and GraphRAG. Build a document Q&A system by hand and validate retrieval with an evaluation dataset; LlamaIndex is a good reference. Agent engineering Planning, tool calling, memory, multi-agent systems and secure deployment. I recommend reading Building Effective Agents. AI evaluation and observability Evaluation datasets, LLM-as-judge, tracing and error analysis. Without evaluation you cannot tell whether a change made things better or worse; see Ragas and Langfuse. Deployment engineering for AI applications Service deployment, concurrent streaming, monitoring, cost and model rollback. The fastest way to grow is to deploy a small project for real and hand it to others to use.

docs.title: Specialization Tracks
docs.text:
“Every man to his trade.”

Nobody can study every field during an undergraduate degree, and there is no need to. Choose one or two directions based on the intersection of your interests, research goals and career plans, and keep going deep. A simple entry standard: you can read classic papers, reproduce a small experiment, and state clearly the core problems and trade-offs of the field. Do not worry if you have not figured it out yet — build solid fundamentals, and most doors will open for you.

Course Description Artificial intelligence and machine learning Deep learning, reinforcement learning, LLMs and multimodality. Start with Andrew Ng's Machine Learning Specialization, then go deeper with CS231n and CS224n. For reinforcement learning, you can begin with the Chinese open source tutorial Easy RL (the "Mushroom Book"); see RL-101: Easy RL. Software engineering and application development Front end, back end, full stack, architecture and cloud-native development. Start with The Odin Project or Full Stack Open, writing and deploying as you go. Computer systems Architecture, compilation, parallelism and kernel development. I recommend UCB CS61C and the legendary CSAPP; for parallelism, see CMU 15-418. Distributed systems and cloud computing Consistency, consensus, algorithms and large-scale system design. First choice is MIT 6.5840, whose five labs take you through building a Raft-based KV store. Computer networks and information security Network protocols, cryptography, web and system security. For theory, see UCB CS161; for hands-on labs, follow SEED Labs. Computer vision Image processing, detection and segmentation, 3D vision and video. The gateway course is Stanford CS231n, whose assignments implement backpropagation and convolution from scratch. Natural language processing Language models, sequence modeling, information extraction and retrieval. I recommend Stanford CS224n; for a next step, take Hugging Face's NLP Course. Robotics and autonomous systems Motion planning, control, SLAM and autonomous driving. Start with UPenn's Robotics Specialization; for SLAM, read Gao Xiang's 14 Lectures on Visual SLAM. Computer graphics and game development Rendering, ray tracing, shaders and game engines. Start with UCB CS184, then work through Ray Tracing in One Weekend. Data science and big data Data analysis, mining, data engineering and stream processing. Get started quickly with Kaggle Learn and enter a competition; for data engineering, see data-engineering-zoomcamp.

docs.title: Career Development and Employment
docs.text:
“Ask not what your company can do for you — ask what you can do for your company.”

Skill and position are not the same thing: many people can write code, but few can explain clearly what they have built and why. The point of this section is to turn your learning into evidence — projects that run, repositories people can read, clear documentation, and the ability to explain your technical choices in an interview. Start accumulating early: preparation for internships and job hunting usually takes several semesters, not a last-minute cram.

Course Description Understanding career paths Learn the responsibilities and requirements of various roles. Read job descriptions on recruiting sites, and use levels.fyi to see the expectations at each level. Projects and portfolio Project selection, deployment and demo, GitHub and technical blogs. A project that can be opened, run and explained clearly is more persuasive than “familiar with technology X.” Internships and job preparation Resumes, algorithmic and engineering interviews, system design interviews. Practice algorithms on LeetCode; for system design, System Design Primer is essential reading. Research and academic development Literature reading, experiment reproduction, paper writing and applications. To begin, read How to Read a Paper; manage references with Zotero, and typeset with LaTeX. Technical communication and teamwork Documentation, code review, project management and presentation. I recommend Google's Technical Writing Courses and its engineering practices. Continuous learning and career growth Tracking trends, evaluating new technology, long-term planning. Read official documentation rather than second-hand tutorials, and follow Hacker News to keep the input flowing.

docs.text:
“Give a man a fish and you feed him for a day; teach a man to fish and you feed him for a lifetime.”

The plan above inevitably reflects strong personal preferences and will not suit everyone; its main purpose is to start a conversation. If you want to pick the directions and material that interest you, the resources listed below are good places to begin.

docs.title: How to Use This Guide
docs.text: As more and more contributors join, the content of this book keeps expanding. Finishing every course in it is neither realistic nor necessary; trying to do so may even backfire and leave you with much effort and little reward. To better match the readers and make this book genuinely useful, I have roughly divided readers into the following three groups according to their needs, so that each of you can plan a self-study program that fits your own situation precisely.

docs.title: Just Started University
docs.text:
If you have just entered university, or are still in your early years and are majoring in computer science or hoping to switch into it, consider yourself lucky, because studying is your main job. You have plenty of time and freedom to learn what interests you, without the pressure of work or the trivialities of daily life, and you need not agonize over utilitarian questions like "will this be useful?" or "will this get me a job?". So how should you arrange your university studies? The first thing, I think, is to break with the step-by-step, follow-the-textbook habit of high school. University is free, in both life and study; there are still classes and exams, but success no longer comes from merely grinding through problem sets. First, you are not limited to the textbook or the classroom — even within your own field you can explore far beyond the syllabus, and you can also learn across disciplines. Second, I hope you will be a little less utilitarian. Having a goal (graduate school, employment, studying abroad) is good, but do not act only to reach it; try instead to learn, in the process, things that will stay with you for a lifetime — a learning method, perhaps, or a way of doing things. Still, being less utilitarian should not become an excuse for laziness and self-indulgence. Finally, balance study and life: studying should be a part of life. In my undergraduate days I joined a club with some almost fanatical people who even slept on the floor of the club room every night; I do not think that was genuine devotion to knowledge, but rather a lack of maturity in how they lived.

This book covers knowledge across the whole field of computing. I suggest you follow your degree plan and take the courses corresponding to your year, while using your spare time to explore courses the classroom does not offer — especially tools and techniques such as Git, Docker and Vue. As things stand, CS education in China does not teach much practical knowledge, yet practice is the most important part of learning in this field, so you will most likely have to do it yourself and accumulate experience bit by bit.

The first thing is to understand what "elegant code" means. Many introductory programming courses in China easily turn into a dry list of syntax rules, less effective than simply having students read the official documentation. In fact, it is very helpful to get a feel, right at the start of programming, for what counts as elegant code and what code "has bad taste". Introductory courses usually begin with procedural programming, such as C, but even in the procedural style you should not lose the habits of modularity and encapsulation. If you write code only to pass an online judge, copying and pasting to pile up one giant main function for convenience, your code quality will quickly settle at that level. Once you meet a slightly bigger project, the cost of debugging, communication and maintenance will snowball. So as you write, ask yourself a few questions: is there a lot of duplication? Is this function doing too many things? The Linux style is to make each function do one thing well. Can this logic be extracted into a separate function? At first it will feel awkward, and you may doubt whether a simple problem is worth all this trouble, but the value of good habits is long-term. C itself is not hard — even a middle schooler can learn it — so why would a company hire you to be a programmer?

After procedural programming, the second semester usually moves on to object orientation, such as C++ or Java. I highly recommend the Notes of MIT 6.031: Software Construction, which uses Java (TypeScript since 2022) to explain in detail how to write more elegant code: test-driven development, the design of function specifications, exception handling, and so on. Since you are touching object orientation, it is also worth learning some common design patterns. Object-oriented courses in China sometimes degenerate into syntax lessons, making students agonize over every way of writing inheritance, with puzzles that resemble brain teasers — things you will almost never use in a real project. What object orientation really trains is the ability to abstract a real problem into a set of classes and the relationships among them; design patterns are abstract lessons distilled by those who came before. Big Talk Design Patterns (《大话设计模式》) is written in a simple, accessible way and makes a good introduction.

The second thing is to learn tools and skills that clearly boost productivity, such as Git, Shell and Vim. I strongly recommend MIT's Missing Semester. It will feel very unfamiliar at first, but force yourself to use these tools for a while, and once you are comfortable your development efficiency will step up noticeably. Many small tools help too. One principle of mine is: any action that takes your hands off the keyboard is worth eliminating. Switching apps, opening files, browsing the web — all can become shortcuts through plugins or tools; on macOS, Alfred is one example. If you repeat an operation every day, and each time it costs more than a second, find a way to cut it to 0.1 seconds. You will be dealing with computers for the next few decades, so forming a smooth workflow early will save you a great deal of effort. Also, learn to touch-type. If you still have to look at the keyboard, find a tutorial right away — it makes a big difference for your efficiency.

The third thing is to balance coursework and self-study. You may question the status quo, but you still have to respect the rules — the GPA carries considerable weight for graduate school admission, after all. So in your first year I would still suggest following your timetable as much as possible, supplemented by high-quality outside resources. For calculus and linear algebra, for example, you can consult the Notes of MIT 18.01/18.02 and MIT 18.06; in the holidays you can learn Python with UCB CS61A. At the same time, gradually build up the programming habits and practical skills mentioned above. In my own experience, mathematics courses carry a high share of credits in the first year, and the exam style varies enormously by school and teacher. Self-study may help you understand the mathematics itself, but it does not necessarily earn you a good grade. So before exams, work through past papers with clear focus to cover the exam-taking side. Once you reach your second year, you can steadily raise the share of self-study, which is likely the safer path.

From the second year on, computer science courses pile up, and that is actually a good time to shift your center of gravity toward self-study. I have organized my three years of self-teaching into a CS study list, briefly describing what each course covers and why it is worth taking. Most of the courses on your timetable will have a foreign counterpart in this list, usually of more solid quality. The core knowledge of computer science is shared to begin with, and good courses tend to explain the principles thoroughly, which many read-the-slides classrooms simply cannot do. Generally speaking, if you pull out the slides the teacher used all semester and cram for two days before the exam, your written score will not look too bad. If a course has a big assignment, you can adapt the labs or projects of a foreign course to meet the course requirements. In short, be flexible: the goal is to master knowledge more efficiently, and when a rule conflicts with that goal, find a way around it or simplify.

Finally, I hope you will be a little less restless and utilitarian, and a little more patient with genuine interest. Many people ask me whether self-study requires exceptional willpower. I think it comes down to what you actually want. If your plan is just that learning a programming language will get you a salary of ten thousand a month, and you are chasing the internet boom, no amount of advice from me will help. When I first started self-studying, I did not think much about utility; it was mostly curiosity, a wish to understand certain things. The whole process was not as grim as it sounds — eat when it is time to eat, play when it is time to play — and looking back, the materials had accumulated all by themselves. Today Sino-American competition is the backdrop, and we are still learning from high-quality foreign courses, admiring how well others do it and feeling a touch of crisis at the same time. So who will change things from here? It still comes down to you, the newcomers. So go for it, young one.

docs.title: Keep the Best, Drop the Rest
docs.text: If you have already finished your undergraduate degree, are studying for a master's, or are already working — perhaps in another field entirely and hoping to make a career change into programming in your spare time — then you probably cannot squeeze out enough time to work systematically through A Learning Plan for Reference Only from beginning to end. Yet you genuinely want to fill in the foundations you missed as an undergraduate. Since readers in this group usually already have some programming experience, introductory courses can be skipped. From a practical standpoint, your career direction is largely settled, and there is no need to go deep into every branch of computing; what is more worth investing in are the principles and skills that generalize widely. So, drawing on my own experience, I have picked a few core courses that I consider the most important and the highest in quality, in the hope of helping you understand computers more deeply. Once you have finished these, whatever your job, you should no longer be someone who merely calls libraries, but someone with a clearer picture of how computers really work underneath.

docs.title: Dreams Have Their Own Destination
docs.text:
If you have a solid command of the core courses in computing and have already settled on your work or research direction, the book still holds many courses that are not mentioned in A Learning Plan for Reference Only for you to explore.

As more contributors join, new branches will keep appearing in the table of contents on the left, such as Advanced Machine Learning and Machine Learning Systems. Under the same branch there are several courses of the same kind, each with a different emphasis and different labs — the Operating Systems branch, for example, includes courses from MIT, Berkeley, Nanjing University and Harbin Institute of Technology. If you want to go deep into a field, studying these parallel courses will give you different perspectives on similar knowledge. The author also plans to invite researchers in relevant fields to share the study and research paths of particular subfields, so that this guide can grow in depth while it expands in breadth.

If you would like to contribute in this area, feel free to contact the author by email at zhangchaowen@stu.scu.edu.cn.

• Offered by: An open source community course by walkinglabs (course website), not a for-credit university course, released as a series of short lessons
  • Prerequisites: A real code repository, familiarity with Git and the command line, and having used at least one coding agent (such as Claude Code or Codex)
  • Programming Languages: None in particular. The course focuses on instruction files, configuration, and verification commands inside a repository, with possibly a little Shell or Python for verification hooks
  • Difficulty: 🌟🌟
  • Class Hour: About 12 lessons, roughly 8 hours of reading, plus at least 15 hours of practice in your own project

This course discusses a very plain question: a capable model does not mean it works reliably in your repository. The word "harness" is used more and more in the AI coding agent community, but most people who say harness actually mean a prompt file. A prompt file is not a harness.

This lesson gives harness a precise, actionable definition. Not an abstract concept from an academic paper, but a framework you can use today. A harness consists of five subsystems: instructions, tools, environment, state, and feedback. Each subsystem has a clear responsibility and clear criteria for judging it.

Learn Harness Engineering is a course focused on putting AI coding agents into production engineering practice. Through deliberate environment design, state management, and verification and control mechanisms, it helps you make AI agents such as Codex and Claude Code reliably complete real engineering tasks. By constraining your AI coding assistant with explicit rules and boundaries, it helps you build features, fix bugs, and automate development tasks more reliably.

The first pitfall in self-study is the lack of a real project. Without a repository to work on, the course quickly degenerates into memorizing concepts, so pick a project you maintain that has some complexity and requires running tests as your practice ground. The second pitfall is over-engineering: trying to build a perfect harness from the start leads to ever more configuration files and verification commands nobody maintains, which only adds burden. The course emphasizes "make it reliable first, then make it elegant", and starting from the smallest workable verification loop is more realistic. The third pitfall is treating second-hand interpretations as course conclusions. Harness Engineering is a recently popular concept whose translations and terminology are not yet unified, and many interpretations exaggerate. When you hit a key claim, go back to the original lessons and OpenAI's harness engineering article to verify it.

docs.title: Why Learn Vim or Emacs
docs.text:
Vim and Emacs bring the following benefits:

  • They keep your fingers on the keyboard for almost the whole development process: Vim's modal editing and Emacs's key binding system both revolve around the keyboard for cursor movement, text manipulation, and command execution, avoiding frequent switching between arrow keys and the mouse so your hands stay in an efficient input state.
  • Convenient file switching and window/buffer management let you work on several files at once, or even several places in the same file: Vim has buffers, windows, and tabs, while Emacs has buffers, windows, and frames, and both organize multi-task editing comfortably.
  • Vim's macros and Emacs's keyboard macros and Elisp scripts can batch repetitive work, such as indenting multiple lines, adding double quotes in bulk, or renaming in bulk, handing mechanical labor to the editor.
  • Vim is the command line editor bundled with many servers, so after you connect to a remote server over ssh there is usually no graphical interface and Vim is ready to use; Emacs also runs in a terminal and can edit remotely through mechanisms such as TRAMP, making it equally suited to environments without a GUI.
  • An extraordinarily rich plugin/extension ecosystem gives you the fanciest terminal editor combinations in the world: Vim has a huge plugin catalog and Emacs has a vast Elisp package ecosystem, and both can be reshaped into a development environment that fits your personal workflow.
  • Deep customization: Vim is configured through vimrc, Vimscript, and Lua, while Emacs is configured through init.el and Elisp, and both can be polished into a personal tool.

docs.title: How to Learn
docs.text:
Unfortunately the learning curve for Vim (or Emacs) really is steep, and it took me several weeks to gradually get used to developing with Vim. At first it feels very uncomfortable, but once you get past the initial stage, believe me, you will love them.

Vim and Emacs are two editors older than most readers. Vim's predecessor vi was born in Berkeley in 1976, and Emacs's prototype appeared even earlier at MIT's AI Lab, where Richard Stallman later organized it into GNU Emacs. They survive today not out of nostalgia but because they held on long enough to a direction almost every editor has abandoned: break editing down into the smallest atomic operations composable from the keyboard, then let users assemble them.

Vim's answer is to split editing into "modes". In normal mode keys are not for typing characters but for actions: d is the delete operator, w is the text object "next word", so dw deletes one word, and ci" means "change the contents inside quotes". The benefit of this compositional grammar is unlimited derivation; once familiar, editing turns from character-by-character movement into a single operation on a structure. The price is a steep learning curve, with efficiency dropping noticeably in the first two weeks.

Emacs's answer is not modes but a programmable runtime environment. It is essentially a Lisp interpreter whose first application happens to be an editor, so key binding enumeration, buffers, windows, and even mail, calendars, and terminals all live under the same set of abstractions. This "editor as operating system" route gives Emacs almost no ceiling on customization, and org-mode grew out of that culture: a plain text markup format that nonetheless handles notes, to-dos, schedules, table calculations, and code block execution.

Neither is the easy choice. The point of this chapter is not to convince you to switch editors but to provide an ordered learning path so you can learn while using it in a real project instead of getting stuck in configuration. The most important principle when learning is: learn to use it first, then learn to configure it. Most Vim plugins merely wrap built-in features, and most Emacs distributions (such as Doom, Spacemacs, and Centaur) package other people's configurations for you, and applying them directly leaves you helpless when something breaks.

• Offered by: The Learn Git Branching open source interactive tutorial (course website), published as a visual sandbox that runs inside the browser
  • Prerequisites: No experience with Git or a graphical client is required; you only need to be able to use a command line (knowing basics such as cd and ls) and to have a rough idea that "version control" exists to keep a history of versions
  • Difficulty: 🌟
  • Class Hour: About 8 hours for the main and remote repository parts, or 15 hours to read everything and finish all the challenge levels

It turns Git's branch operations into playable levels. The tutorial is organized around several core level groups: the basics cover commit, branch, merge, and rebase; the advanced part covers checkout, reset, revert, cherry-pick, and interactive rebase for moving between commits; then come groups on "moving commits around", "miscellaneous", and "advanced topics", and finally the remote repository part covering clone, fetch, pull, push, tracking branches, and remote branches. Each level has one clear goal, with a visual repository graph on the right; once you type a command, the commit nodes and branch pointers move immediately, and reaching the goal completes the level. Progress is stored locally in the browser.

Its biggest strength is turning the abstract branch model directly into an image. The most confusing part of Git is the mental model where "commits are nodes, branches are pointers, and HEAD is the current position", and no amount of writing that in a handout beats actually using git rebase to attach a detached commit onto another branch and watching the nodes rearrange in the graph. Second, every level demonstrates first and then asks you to practice, with a short explanation and command hints on the left and undo and reset always available on the right, so failure costs nothing; you can experiment boldly in a way that is impossible in a real repository. Compared with systematic texts such as Pro Git, it does not walk through principles and configuration item by item; compared with scattered Git cheatsheets, it offers a progressive order and immediate feedback.

• Offered by: Compiled from the official LaTeX project and Chinese material from the CTEX community (LaTeX project)

LaTeX is a typesetting system built on TeX. Knuth developed TeX and Lamport wrapped LaTeX around it, both towering figures in computing. But famous authors are not a reason to learn it. What separates it from WYSIWYG software like Word is the division of labor: you write the content and the system handles typesetting. Heading levels, figure numbering, formula spacing, and bibliography formatting are all governed by style rules, so someone with no typesetting experience can still produce professionally laid out documents.

That trait shows most clearly in long documents. By the hundredth page, manual formatting costs rise exponentially, whereas LaTeX keeps every new section consistent with the style defined at the start, with numbering and tables of contents updating automatically. Mathematics is its traditional strength, and complex fractions, matrices, and multiple subscripts are naturally easier to write than in any GUI.

The path is fairly clear, and the hard part is at the start. Environment setup is the first blocker, since a local TeX distribution often lacks packages and fonts; an online editor such as Overleaf skips this step and ships plenty of ready templates.

• Offered by: Compiled from the official Scoop documentation and community practice (Scoop website)
  • Prerequisites: Familiarity with basic PowerShell usage on Windows and an idea of what environment variables are
  • Difficulty: 🌟

Setting up a development environment on Windows has always been a nuisance. Without a common standard, every tool installs differently: some need a download and a few clicks, some need manual extraction and environment variables, and ten tools can eat an entire day. Scoop removes those differences, managing common command line tools centrally so installation and upgrades take one command and environment variables are handled for you.

Getting started is trivial; installing Python and Node.js takes two lines:

scoop install python
scoop install nodejs

Scoop itself needs PowerShell 5.1 or later. Windows 10 and newer ship with it, while the version built into Windows 7 is too old and must be upgraded first. One detail that trips up many users in China: people often set a Chinese username when creating their Windows account, which makes the user directory a Chinese path, and since Scoop installs into the user directory by default, some software fails to run there. It is better to install into a custom all-English directory with -ScoopDir:

Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser
irm get.scoop.sh -outfile 'install.ps1'
.\install.ps1 -ScoopDir 'C:\Scoop'

Its main benefit is turning software installation into a repeatable, portable action. On a new machine, rerun your installation list to restore the environment instead of recalling what option you chose for every installer years ago.

docs.text: The next step is bucket management. Write the tools you always install into a manifest script and keep it in your dotfiles, and setting up a new machine stops being repetitive work.

• Offered by: The open source course Context-Engineering initiated by davidkimai (course website), with the original material hosted in the GitHub repository
  • Prerequisites: Familiarity with prompt engineering basics (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought), Python, and at least one LLM API; chapters on memory, RAG, and agents assume an understanding of vector retrieval and tool calling
  • Programming Languages: Python, with examples in the guides provided as notebook-style single-file scripts and configuration files written in YAML
  • Difficulty: 🌟🌟🌟🌟
  • Class Hour: The course describes a 12-week staged learning path, roughly 50 to 70 hours at 4 to 6 hours a week; the foundations and system implementation parts alone take about 20 hours for a first pass

The core claim is that prompt engineering only addresses what you say, while context engineering addresses everything else the model sees. The author cites Karpathy's definition, that context engineering is "the delicate art and science of filling the context window with just the right information for the next step", and adopts the framing of A Survey of Context Engineering (a review of more than 1,400 papers): context is not just the prompt the user sends, but the complete information payload provided to the model at inference time, covering examples, memory, retrieved documents, tools, state, and control flow. The course builds a progressive four-level structure on a biological metaphor: atoms (single instructions and simple constraints), molecules (few-shot examples and demonstration sets), cells (persistent memory, state management, the context window), and organs (multi-step flows, specialists, system orchestration). Above that sit neural systems and semantic fields (reasoning frameworks, verification tools, cognitive patterns, attractors and resonance), then protocol shells and a unified system, and finally a meta-recursive framework of self-reflection, recursive improvement, and interpretable evolution. Each level maps onto a real technical form, from basic prompt engineering all the way to multi-agent systems and self-organizing systems.

Compared with similar material, its most striking feature is treating context as an engineering object to be measured, pruned, and orchestrated rather than a bag of prompting tricks. The course states six methodological rules: start from first principles, add only what the model demonstrably lacks, quantify token cost, latency, and quality score, delete ruthlessly because pruning beats padding, prefer code to slides with a runnable cell for every concept, and visualize everything with ASCII and symbolic diagrams. It also embeds recent research directly into the material. MEM1 merges memory and reasoning; IBM Zurich's cognitive tools treat structured prompt templates as tool calls, raising GPT-4.1's pass@1 on AIME2024 from 26.7% to 43.3%; ICML Princeton's three-stage attention architecture of emergent symbolic mechanisms explains why structured formats such as Markdown and JSON parse more easily.

The experience clearly has two tracks. The first three layers, from atoms to organs, are very practical: with the 00_foundations, 10_guides_zero_to_one, 20_templates, and 30_examples directories you can drop a context template into your own project the same day. The later half on field theory, protocol shells, and meta-recursion is more speculative, leans heavily on physics and biology metaphors, and reads like an essay on ideas rather than a tutorial. The author calls it a frontier, first-principles handbook with many chapters still being built, so do not expect the tight chain of derivations you would get from a textbook.

The first pitfall is mistaking the metaphor for a conclusion. The atoms, molecules, cells analogy is useful for intuition, but claims like "context is a field" or "meaning depends on the observer" are still research hypotheses, and practical work should return to concrete actions: how to prune, how to retrieve, how to evaluate. The second pitfall is piling on features without measurement. The course keeps stressing the three-way trade-off between token budget, latency, and quality; without your own evaluation loop it is easy to build a system whose context grows longer while results grow worse, which Chroma's Context Rot research documents. The third pitfall is the fast-moving repository. Directory names, script paths, and chapter numbering shift as the material evolves (the README itself shows both 10_guides_zero_to_hero and 10_guides_zero_to_one), so check the current file tree when links break, and use DeepWiki's question answering to locate the latest content. The fourth pitfall is treating it as a replacement for prompt engineering. The right order is to get a stable base prompt first and then orchestrate context; when the base prompt is already unclear, adding memory and retrieval only amplifies the confusion.
