docs.text:
• Offered by: The open source project Prompt Engineering Guide initiated by DAIR.AI (Chinese site, English site), continuously updated as an online handbook and backed by a GitHub repository
  • Prerequisites: No machine learning background is required; being able to use any large language model (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Kimi, DeepSeek, and so on) is enough to start. Reading the "Models" and "Research" sections goes more smoothly with basic familiarity with Transformers and attention
  • Programming Languages: The guide is mostly prompt text and does not force you to write code; chapters such as RAG, ReAct, and Program-Aided Language Models include Python examples, and the Notebooks section provides runnable OpenAI API code
  • Difficulty: 🌟🌟
  • Class Hour: About 20 hours to read through, or more than 40 hours including hands-on experimentation (reproducing the prompts in each technique chapter yourself)

The content unfolds in three layers. The first is the introduction: what prompt engineering is, basic concepts, prompt elements (instruction, context, input data, output format), how to tune model settings (temperature, top-p, max length), general tips for designing prompts, and a large set of prompt examples. The second layer is the core, the "Prompting Techniques" section: starting from zero-shot and few-shot prompting and progressing to chain-of-thought (CoT), self-consistency, tree of thoughts (ToT), generated knowledge, prompt chaining, retrieval augmented generation (RAG), the ReAct framework, Reflexion, automatic reasoning and tool-use (ART), automatic prompt engineer (APE), directional stimulus prompting, and program-aided language models. Each technique is presented as motivation, implementation, experimental findings, and limitations. The third layer covers applications and context: the Prompt Hub library of task-organized templates (classification, coding, question answering, reasoning, summarization, information extraction, adversarial prompting), introductions to mainstream models (GPT-4, LLaMA, Gemini, Mistral, Mixtral, Claude, Kimi), risks and misuse (bias, factuality, jailbreaking and prompt injection), and the recently added Agent and context engineering series (Introduction to Agents, Agent Components, Context Engineering, Deep Agents, Function Calling).

Its main strength is the concept-example-paper triad. Each technique gets a one-line intuition, a prompt you can copy directly, and then the experimental setup and results from the original paper, so you learn why the trick works and when it breaks down. Compared with scattered blog posts and short videos, it is systematic, cited, and evidence-backed; compared with going straight to the papers, it lays out the terminology and motivation first, which lowers the barrier a lot. The Chinese and English sites track each other closely, with most technique chapters translated into Chinese and technical terms kept in English parentheses for easy cross-checking against the original literature.

The experience is "easy at the start, self-directed further in". The first dozen pages need no background at all, and within half an hour you are already editing your own prompts, which is immediately rewarding. Further in it becomes more research-oriented: tree of thoughts, self-consistency, and directional stimulus prompting cite a fair number of paper conclusions, and readers unused to experiment tables can get stuck in the details. Treat it as a searchable roadmap rather than a linear textbook: read through once for the framework, then come back to the relevant chapter when you have a real task.

The first pitfall is memorizing templates without understanding the motivation. Copying prompts from the Prompt Hub is satisfying, but they fail as soon as the task changes, because what does the work is the structure (role, task description, context, output constraints) rather than any particular wording. After copying a template, rewrite it yourself and see which parts cannot be moved. The second pitfall is ignoring model differences. Most examples were validated on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4; move to a domestic or small local model and the number of few-shot examples or the trigger words for CoT may behave completely differently, so re-test on your target model. The third pitfall is treating prompting tricks as a universal solution. CoT genuinely helps on reasoning problems, but it does not remove hallucination in factual question answering; when RAG or tool calling is the right tool, switch to it, as the guide itself repeatedly points out. The fourth pitfall is content drift caused by the site's evolution. The newly added Agent and Context Engineering chapters are not fully consistent in terminology and recommendations with the earlier model chapters, and some new pages on the Chinese site still show English titles; when you hit a dated page (say one that only discusses GPT-3), switch to the English site or check the current state of the GitHub repository.

• Offered by: The open source tutorial Hello Algo (course website), written by Jin Yudong (Krahets) and released as an open source e-book
  • Prerequisites: Basic syntax of any programming language (variables, loops, functions, recursion), plus an intuitive grasp of arrays and linked lists
  • Programming Languages: Examples cover more than ten languages, including Java, C++, Python, Go, JavaScript, TypeScript, C#, Rust, Swift, Dart, and Zig, with every piece of logic provided in multiple languages
  • Difficulty: 🌟🌟
  • Class Hour: About 40 hours to read through, or more than 60 hours including hands-on implementation and practice problems

The book has three major parts: complexity analysis, data structures, and algorithms. The data structure part covers arrays and linked lists, stacks and queues, hash tables, binary trees, heaps, and graphs, while the algorithm part covers searching, sorting, divide and conquer, backtracking, dynamic programming, and greedy algorithms. Each chapter follows a "definition, implementation, use cases" order: a knowledge map first, then each structure dismantled one by one, and finally the algorithmic paradigms tying it together. It works well as your first book on the subject.

Its most distinctive feature is animated illustrations with runnable code. Every key operation has a frame-by-frame animation that walks you through how the data changes in memory, which builds intuition more easily than static diagrams. All example code runs as-is, is heavily commented, and the same logic is given in a dozen languages so you can read along in the one you know. Compared with theory- and proof-heavy texts such as Introduction to Algorithms, it reads more like a route you can walk while typing; compared with scattered interview notes, it is systematic and selective instead of piling up tricks from page one.

The learning curve really is smooth: short chapters, plenty of figures, little prose, and a chapter a day is rarely a struggle. It is very friendly to readers with no prior background. But be clear about its scope. It is an introductory book: advanced structures such as red-black trees, B-trees, union-find, and segment trees are not covered, complexity derivations stay shallow, and dynamic programming only reaches the classic models. After finishing it you can read most editorials, but it is not enough by itself for contests or the hard half of algorithm interviews at large companies, and another more demanding course should follow.

The first pitfall is mistaking understanding the animation for having mastered the topic. Animations are intuitive enough to create an illusion, and only when you actually write the code do you find that boundary conditions, array indices, and recursion base cases cannot be skipped. Close the book and implement each section yourself. The second pitfall is the lack of a companion exercise set. The book explains principles and does not supply enough problems, so pair it with LeetCode problems organized by topic, otherwise fluency never forms. The third pitfall is distraction from multi-language examples. Stick to one language at the beginner stage instead of cross-referencing several, or your attention drifts to syntax differences rather than the algorithm itself.

• Offered by: OI Wiki an open source knowledge base (course website) maintained by contributors under the CC BY-SA 4.0 license with English content updated continuously
  • Prerequisites: Basic C/C++ syntax and standard library, familiarity with the basic operations on arrays and strings, and the ability to read complexity notation
  • Programming Languages: Mostly C++, with some entries also available in Python and Java, in a contest-oriented coding style
  • Difficulty: 🌟🌟🌟🌟
  • Class Hour: About 80 hours for a systematic read of the basic and advanced parts, or more than 150 hours to go deep by topic with targeted practice

OI Wiki is a knowledge base for competitive programming (OI). Instead of being taught over a semester, it organizes topics as encyclopedic entries. The content falls into three blocks. The basics cover language fundamentals, complexity analysis, enumeration, simulation, recursion, greedy algorithms, binary search, searching, introductory dynamic programming, and string basics. The advanced part covers dynamic programming variants such as bitmask DP, tree DP, and slope optimization, plus data structures including union-find, Fenwick trees, segment trees, and balanced trees, along with graph modeling, network flow, and a wide range of string algorithms. The mathematics and contest-technique block covers number theory, combinatorics, linear algebra, polynomials, and game theory, as well as how these data structures and algorithms combine in real problems.

Its defining trait is completeness and depth. Topics almost absent from textbooks yet repeatedly tested in contests, such as persistent segment trees, link-cut trees, dynamic trees, and the Min_25 sieve, each have their own entry with derivations, template code, and linked examples, spanning everything from beginner level to provincial team and beyond. An entry typically states the definition and the naive idea first, then derives the optimization, and finally gives complexity and a code template, with references in the footer so you can follow the trail to original papers and blogs. Compared with introductory books such as Hello Algo, it does not aim for a smooth learning curve; compared with scattered contest blogs, it keeps terminology consistent and structure clear, so a tool does not change names and implementations from page to page, which matters a lot for building a coherent framework.

The reading experience is closer to a reference manual than a textbook. Individual entries are dense with formulas and code and lack narrative continuity or designed exercises, so a first pass is hard to read straight through. It is better used with specific questions in hand. The upside is that you jump straight to what you need rather than following a fixed chapter order; the downside is fragmentation, where you have read the definition of a balanced tree but cannot write a rotation, or know the network flow template but cannot tell which problems should be modeled that way. Use it as a dictionary and a tool for deep dives into individual topics, and pair it with a tutorial or course that provides a teaching order and the big picture.

The first pitfall is diving into advanced entries without filtering prerequisites. Segment trees and balanced trees assume you are comfortable with recursion, tree structures, and pointer manipulation; jumping straight into the templates only lets you memorize code without understanding it, so first work through the basics plus recursion, binary search, and union-find. The second pitfall is treating templates as answers. The OI Wiki templates are usually not the optimal implementation, and copying them blindly skips the reasoning and leaves you unable to transfer the idea to variants, so re-implement every template yourself and rename the variables to understand the details. The third pitfall is ignoring the mathematics entries. Number theory, combinatorics, and matrix exponentiation are often the dividing line in contests and the driest to read, so look them up when a problem type demands them instead of reading them front to back, which usually ends in abandoning them.

• Offered by: The Datawhale open source community tutorial Easy RL: A Tutorial on Reinforcement Learning (commonly known as the "Mushroom Book", course website), written by Wang Qi, Yang Yiyuan, and Jiang Ji, with a print edition published by Posts and Telecom Press
  • Prerequisites: Comfortable with Python, basic probability (random variables, expectation, conditional probability), linear algebra and calculus, and common deep learning background (neural networks, backpropagation, gradient descent)
  • Programming Languages: Python, with code mainly based on PyTorch and Gym
  • Difficulty: 🌟🌟🌟
  • Class Hour: About 60 hours to read through, or more than 100 hours including running the algorithms and working through the exercises

The course has two major parts. Part one (chapters 1 to 3) builds the foundation: how reinforcement learning differs from other machine learning paradigms, then Markov decision processes (MP, MRP, and MDP in increasing layers), and tabular methods (Q tables, Sarsa, Q-learning, policy evaluation and improvement). Part two (chapters 4 to 13) moves into deep reinforcement learning, covering model-free prediction and control, deep learning basics, DQN and its variants, DQN for continuous actions, policy gradient, Actor-Critic, DDPG, PPO, and practical problems such as sparse rewards and imitation learning. The chapters of part two are relatively independent and can be read selectively, which gives readers with different goals room to choose.

Its main strengths are being Chinese-language, systematic, and exercise-backed. The book started as an organized expansion of Hung-yi Lee's open course on deep reinforcement learning along with lecture notes from Bolei Zhou, David Silver, and others, filling in derivations that jump abruptly in the videos. Every chapter ends with exercises and solutions, so it does not read like a scattered survey. Compared with Sutton's Reinforcement Learning, which is theory-first and extremely dense, it leans toward engineering implementation and intuition building. Compared with open source RL code repositories, it does not skip steps and explains why each algorithm is designed the way it is. The community consensus is that the book is readable, and I think that comes from keeping the derivations while pairing them with many figures and plain Chinese explanations.

The experience has a clear steep section. The first three chapters are easy going, but once DQN arrives, target networks, experience replay, temporal difference, and importance sampling all come at once, and anyone with a shaky deep learning foundation tends to fall behind there. Before starting part two, review neural network training and gradient descent, and think through motivation questions such as why a target network is needed; that is far more effective than memorizing formulas.

The first pitfall is reading without running. Many details of reinforcement learning only surface when the code runs: reward scaling, exploration decay, sample efficiency. Reading alone creates the feeling of understanding, and only a training run that refuses to converge shows where the problem really is. Run at least one environment each for Q-learning, DQN, and PPO. The second pitfall is skipping part one to jump straight into deep reinforcement learning. MDPs, Bellman equations, and temporal difference are the shared language of the field, and a weak grasp there causes repeated stalls later. The third pitfall is being intimidated by the notation. The derivations do require patience, but most steps are basic operations on expectations and gradients; when stuck, revisit the first two chapters or compare with Hung-yi Lee's video lectures, where a single sentence often clears it up. One final warning: the book was written a few years ago, so some library versions and code interfaces have changed, and you should follow the most recent branch of the official repository when running the code.
